bio: XI Ch 1: The Living World
Ernst Mayr (1904–2004), born on 5 July 1904 in Kempten, Germany, is known as 'The Darwin of the 20th century'.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Ernst Mayr pioneered the currently accepted biological concept of species and made the origin of species diversity the central question of evolutionary biology.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Ernst Mayr was awarded the 'triple crown of biology': the Balzan Prize (1983), the International Prize for Biology (1994), and the Crafoord Prize (1999).
XI Ch 1: The Living World
The number of species that are known and described ranges between 1.7–1.8 million, which refers to biodiversity.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
ICBN stands for International Code for Botanical Nomenclature, which provides agreed principles and criteria for naming plants.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
ICZN stands for International Code of Zoological Nomenclature, evolved by animal taxonomists for naming animals.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Binomial nomenclature, given by Carolus Linnaeus, is the system of providing a scientific name with two components: Generic name and specific epithet.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
In Mangifera indica Linn., Mangifera represents the genus, indica is the specific epithet, and Linn. indicates the species was first described by Linnaeus.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Biological names are generally in Latin and printed in italics, or separately underlined when handwritten to indicate their Latin origin.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
The first word denoting the genus starts with a capital letter, while the specific epithet starts with a small letter.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature are the four processes that are basic to taxonomy.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
The word 'systematics' is derived from the Latin word 'systema' meaning systematic arrangement of organisms; Carolus Linnaeus used Systema Naturae as the title of his publication.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Systematics takes into account evolutionary relationships between organisms in addition to identification, nomenclature and classification.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
The taxonomic hierarchy in ascending order is: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum (for animals) or Division (for plants) → Kingdom.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
As we go higher from species to kingdom in the taxonomic hierarchy, the number of common characteristics goes on decreasing.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Lower the taxa, more are the characteristics that the members within the taxon share; higher the category, greater is the difficulty of determining relationships to other taxa at the same level.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Genus Solanum includes species like tuberosum (potato), nigrum (makoi) and melongena (brinjal).
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Genus Panthera includes lion (Panthera leo), leopard (P. pardus) and tiger (P. tigris), whereas cats belong to the genus Felis.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Three different plant genera Solanum, Petunia and Datura are placed in the family Solanaceae.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Plant families Convolvulaceae and Solanaceae are included in the order Polymoniales mainly based on floral characters.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
The animal order Carnivora includes families like Felidae and Canidae; class Mammalia includes order Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) and order Carnivora.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Man (Homo sapiens): Genus Homo, Family Hominidae, Order Primata, Class Mammalia, Phylum Chordata.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Housefly (Musca domestica): Genus Musca, Family Muscidae, Order Diptera, Class Insecta, Phylum Arthropoda.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Mango (Mangifera indica): Genus Mangifera, Family Anacardiaceae, Order Sapindales, Class Dicotyledonae, Division Angiospermae.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Wheat (Triticum aestivum): Genus Triticum, Family Poaceae, Order Poales, Class Monocotyledonae, Division Angiospermae.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Mayr joined Harvard’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences in 1953 and retired in 1975, assuming the title Alexander Agassiz Professor of Zoology Emeritus.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Throughout his nearly 80-year career, his research spanned ornithology, taxonomy, zoogeography, evolution, systematics, and the history and philosophy of biology.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Mayr died at the age of 100 in the year 2004.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Each different kind of plant, animal or organism that you see, represents a species.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
The scientific names ensure that each organism has only one name.
XI Ch 1: The Living World
Description of any organism should enable the people (in any part of the world) to arrive at the same name.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Aristotle was the earliest to attempt a more scientific basis for classification, dividing plants into trees, shrubs and herbs and animals into those with red blood and those without.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed a Five Kingdom Classification: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
The main criteria used by R.H. Whittaker for the five-kingdom classification include cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
The three-domain system divides Kingdom Monera into two domains, leaving the remaining eukaryotic kingdoms in the third domain, resulting in a six-kingdom classification.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
In the Five Kingdom system, Kingdom Monera has prokaryotic cells with a noncellulosic cell wall composed of polysaccharide + amino acid (peptidoglycan) and cellular body organisation.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Kingdom Protista consists of unicellular eukaryotes, Kingdom Fungi has chitinous cell walls and loose tissue body organisation, Kingdom Plantae has cellulosic cell walls, and Kingdom Animalia lacks cell walls and shows holozoic nutrition.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Bacteria are grouped under four categories based on shape: spherical Coccus, rod-shaped Bacillus, comma-shaped Vibrium, and spiral Spirillum.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Bacteria as a group show the most extensive metabolic diversity, whereas their structure is very simple.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Archaebacteria live in harsh habitats: halophiles in extreme salty areas, thermoacidophiles in hot springs, and methanogens in marshy areas.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Archaebacteria differ from other bacteria in having a different cell wall structure, which is responsible for their survival in extreme conditions.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Methanogens are present in the gut of ruminant animals such as cows and buffaloes and produce methane (biogas) from their dung.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) have chlorophyll a similar to green plants and are photosynthetic autotrophs; some fix atmospheric nitrogen in specialised cells called heterocysts (e.g., Nostoc and Anabaena).
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria oxidise inorganic substances such as nitrates, nitrites and ammonia for ATP production and play a great role in recycling nitrogen, phosphorous, iron and sulphur.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Cholera, typhoid, tetanus and citrus canker are well-known diseases caused by different heterotrophic bacteria.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Mycoplasma completely lack a cell wall, are the smallest living cells known, can survive without oxygen, and are pathogenic in animals and plants.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Chrysophytes include diatoms and golden algae (desmids); in diatoms, cell walls form two thin overlapping shells embedded with silica that fit together like a soap box.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Diatom cell wall deposits accumulated over billions of years form 'diatomaceous earth', used in polishing and filtration of oils and syrups; diatoms are the chief 'producers' in the oceans.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Dinoflagellates are mostly marine and photosynthetic with stiff cellulose plates on the outer cell wall and two flagella (one longitudinal and one transverse in a furrow between wall plates).
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Red dinoflagellates like Gonyaulax undergo rapid multiplication making the sea appear red (red tides) and release toxins that kill marine animals such as fishes.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Euglenoids (e.g., Euglena) are fresh water organisms found in stagnant water that lack a cell wall and instead have a protein-rich layer called pellicle which makes their body flexible.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Slime moulds are saprophytic protists that form an aggregation called plasmodium under suitable conditions and differentiate into spore-bearing fruiting bodies with true walls during unfavourable conditions.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Four major groups of protozoans are: Amoeboid protozoans (e.g., Amoeba, parasitic Entamoeba), Flagellated protozoans (e.g., Trypanosoma causing sleeping sickness), Ciliated protozoans (e.g., Paramoecium with a gullet), and Sporozoans (e.g., Plasmodium causing malaria).
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Fungi have cell walls composed of chitin and polysaccharides; their bodies consist of slender thread-like hyphae forming a network called mycelium, which may be aseptate multinucleate (coenocytic) or septate.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
The fungal sexual cycle involves three steps: (i) Plasmogamy (fusion of protoplasms), (ii) Karyogamy (fusion of two nuclei), and (iii) Meiosis in zygote resulting in haploid spores.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
In ascomycetes and basidiomycetes, an intervening dikaryotic stage (n + n, two nuclei per cell) called dikaryophase occurs before parental nuclei fuse.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Phycomycetes have aseptate and coenocytic mycelium and reproduce asexually by motile zoospores or non-motile aplanospores produced endogenously in a sporangium; examples include Mucor, Rhizopus (bread mould) and Albugo (parasitic fungus on mustard).
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Ascomycetes (sac-fungi) have branched, septate mycelium, produce asexual conidia exogenously on conidiophores and sexual ascospores endogenously in sac-like asci arranged in ascocarps; examples include Yeast (Saccharomyces, unicellular), Penicillium, Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora (used in biochemical and genetic work), and edible morels and truffles.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Basidiomycetes (mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs) have branched, septate mycelium, lack sex organs, form dikaryotic structure by somatogamy, and produce four exogenous basidiospores on a basidium in basidiocarps; examples include Agaricus (mushroom), Ustilago (smut) and Puccinia (rust fungus).
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Deuteromycetes are called imperfect fungi because only their asexual or vegetative phases (reproducing by conidia) are known; examples include Alternaria, Colletotrichum and Trichoderma.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Dmitri Ivanowsky (1892) recognised certain microbes smaller than bacteria as causal organisms of tobacco mosaic disease; M.W. Beijerinck (1898) called the infectious fluid 'Contagium vivum fluidum'; W.M. Stanley (1935) showed viruses could be crystallised and crystals consist largely of proteins.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

No virus contains both RNA and DNA; plant viruses generally have single-stranded RNA, while bacteriophages usually have double-stranded DNA enclosed in a protein coat called capsid made of subunits called capsomeres.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Viroids were discovered by T.O. Diener in 1971 as a free RNA of low molecular weight lacking a protein coat; they cause potato spindle tuber disease.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Prions are infectious neurological disease-transmitting agents consisting of abnormally folded protein similar in size to viruses, causing bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease) in cattle and Creutzfeldt–Jacob disease (CJD) in humans.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification

Lichens are symbiotic associations between an autotrophic algal component (phycobiont) and a heterotrophic fungal component (mycobiont); they are very good pollution indicators as they do not grow in polluted areas.
XI Ch 2: Biological Classification
Since the dawn of civilisation, there have been many attempts to classify living organisms.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

Artificial systems of classification (e.g., by Linnaeus based on androecium structure) used gross superficial morphological characters and gave equal weightage to vegetative and sexual characteristics.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

Natural classification systems for flowering plants, based on natural affinities including external features, ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology and phytochemistry, were given by George Bentham and Joseph Dalton Hooker.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Numerical Taxonomy uses computers to assign numbers and codes to all observable characteristics, giving each character equal importance.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Cytotaxonomy is based on cytological information like chromosome number, structure and behaviour, whereas Chemotaxonomy uses chemical constituents of plants to resolve confusions.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
In algae, sexual reproduction is isogamous with flagellated gametes in Ulothrix, isogamous with non-flagellated gametes in Spirogyra, anisogamous in Eudorina, and oogamous in Volvox and Fucus.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

At least half of the total carbon dioxide fixation on earth is carried out by algae through photosynthesis; about 70 species of marine algae including Porphyra, Laminaria and Sargassum are used as food.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Hydrocolloids (water-holding substances) are produced by marine algae: algin from brown algae and carrageen from red algae.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

Agar, obtained from red algae Gelidium and Gracilaria, is used to grow microbes and in preparations of ice-creams and jellies; Chlorella is a unicellular protein-rich green alga used as a food supplement by space travellers.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

Chlorophyceae (green algae) possess chlorophyll a and b, store food as starch in pyrenoids (which contain protein besides starch), have an inner cell wall of cellulose and outer layer of pectose, and have 2–8 equal, apical flagella; examples: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra and Chara.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

Phaeophyceae (brown algae) possess chlorophyll a, c, carotenoids and fucoxanthin (xanthophyll), store food as laminarin or mannitol, have a cellulosic cell wall covered by algin, and have 2 unequal, lateral flagella on pyriform zoospores/gametes; examples: Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum and Fucus.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

Rhodophyceae (red algae) possess chlorophyll a, d and r-phycoerythrin, store food as floridean starch (very similar to amylopectin and glycogen in structure), have cell walls of cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters, and lack flagellated stages completely; examples: Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria and Gelidium.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Bryophytes (mosses and liverworts) are called amphibians of the plant kingdom because they live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

In bryophytes, the main plant body is a haploid gametophyte bearing multicellular male antheridia (producing biflagellate antherozoids) and flask-shaped female archegonia (producing a single egg); the sporophyte is attached to and dependent on the photosynthetic gametophyte.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Sphagnum, a moss, provides peat used as fuel and as packing material for trans-shipment of living material because of its capacity to hold water.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Liverworts (e.g., Marchantia) have a dorsiventral thalloid body and reproduce asexually by green, multicellular asexual buds called gemmae formed in gemma cups.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

The gametophyte of mosses consists of two stages: a creeping, green, branched, filamentous protonema stage (developing directly from a spore) and an upright leafy stage (developing from secondary protonema as a lateral bud) bearing spirally arranged leaves and multicellular branched rhizoids; examples: Funaria, Polytrichum and Sphagnum.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

Pteridophytes (horsetails and ferns) are the first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues —xylem and phloem—and their main plant body is a diploid sporophyte differentiated into true root, stem and leaves.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Leaves in pteridophyta are small (microphylls) as in Selaginella or large (macrophylls) as in ferns; sporophylls may form compact strobili or cones in Selaginella and Equisetum.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Spores of pteridophytes germinate to form an inconspicuous, small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid gametophyte called prothallus.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

Majority of pteridophytes are homosporous, whereas genera like Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous (producing macro and micro spores); retention of the female gametophyte on the parent sporophyte for variable periods is a precursor to the seed habit.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Four classes of Pteridophytes are: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), and Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum).
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Gymnosperms have naked ovules not enclosed by any ovary wall; the giant redwood tree Sequoia is one of the tallest gymnosperm tree species.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Gymnosperm roots are generally tap roots: Pinus has fungal association in the form of mycorrhiza, while Cycas has small specialised coralloid roots associated with N2-fixing cyanobacteria.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Stems are unbranched in Cycas and branched in Pinus and Cedrus; conifer needle-like leaves have a thick cuticle and sunken stomata to reduce water loss.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom

All gymnosperms are heterosporous; male and female cones are borne on the same tree (monoecious) in Pinus, whereas in Cycas male cones and megasporophylls are borne on different trees (dioecious); male and female gametophytes do not have an independent free-living existence.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Angiosperms range in size from the smallest Wolffia to tall trees of Eucalyptus (over 100 metres) and are divided into Dicotyledons and Monocotyledons.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Fungi, and members of the Monera and Protista having cell walls have now been excluded from Plantae though earlier classifications placed them in the same kingdom.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
So, the cyanobacteria that are also referred to as blue green algae are not ‘algae’ any more.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
At present phylogenetic classification systems based on evolutionary relationships between the various organisms are acceptable.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Numerical Taxonomy which is now easily carried out using computers is based on all observable characteristics.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Number and codes are assigned to all the characters and the data are then processed.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
In this way each character is given equal importance and at the same time hundreds of characters can be considered.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and largely aquatic (both fresh water and marine) organisms.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
A few of the marine forms such as kelps, form massive plant bodies.
XI Ch 3: Plant Kingdom
The algae reproduce by vegetative, asexual and sexual methods.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Levels of organisation in Animalia: Porifera (cellular level), Coelenterata and Ctenophora (tissue level), Platyhelminthes (organ and organ-system level), and Aschelminthes to Chordata (organ- system level).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Digestive system is incomplete (single opening serving as both mouth and anus) in Coelenterata, Ctenophora and Platyhelminthes, and complete (two openings, mouth and anus) from Aschelminthes to Chordata.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Sponges are mostly asymmetrical; Coelenterates, Ctenophores and adult Echinoderms (larvae are bilateral) exhibit radial symmetry; Platyhelminthes to Chordata (except adult Echinoderms) exhibit bilateral symmetry.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Diploblastic animals have two embryonic layers (ectoderm and endoderm with undifferentiated mesoglea in between, e.g., Coelenterata and Ctenophora); Triploblastic animals have a third germinal layer, mesoderm (Platyhelminthes to Chordata).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Acoelomates lack a body cavity (Platyhelminthes); Pseudocoelomates have mesoderm as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm (Aschelminthes); Coelomates have a true coelom lined by mesoderm (Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata and Chordata).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Metamerism (metameric segmentation, where the body is externally and internally divided into segments with serial repetition of at least some organs) is exhibited by Annelida, Arthropoda and Chordata.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
Notochord is a mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development in chordates.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Porifera (sponges): have a water transport or canal system where water enters through minute pores (ostia) into a central cavity (spongocoel) and goes out through the osculum; choanocytes or collar cells line the spongocoel and canals.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Porifera have intracellular digestion, a skeleton of spicules or spongin fibres, are hermaphrodite with internal fertilisation and indirect development; examples: Sycon (Scypha), Spongilla (Fresh water sponge) and Euspongia (Bath sponge).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Coelenterata (Cnidaria): possess cnidoblasts or cnidocytes (containing stinging capsules or nematocysts) for anchorage, defense and prey capture, a central gastro-vascular cavity with a single opening (mouth on hypostome), and both extracellular and intracellular digestion.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Cnidarians exhibit two body forms: sessile cylindrical polyp (e.g., Hydra, Adamsia) and umbrella-shaped free-swimming medusa (e.g., Aurelia or jelly fish); forms like Obelia exhibit alternation of generations (Metagenesis) where polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
Examples of Coelenterata: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war), Adamsia (Sea anemone), Pennatula (Sea-pen), Gorgonia (Sea-fan) and Meandrina (Brain coral).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Ctenophora (sea walnuts or comb jellies): exclusively marine, radially symmetrical, diploblastic, bear eight external rows of ciliated comb plates for locomotion, exhibit well-marked bioluminescence, reproduce only sexually with external fertilisation and indirect development; examples: Pleurobrachia and Ctenoplana.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Platyhelminthes (flatworms): dorso-ventrally flattened, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, acoelomate; parasitic forms have hooks and suckers; specialised flame cells help in osmoregulation and excretion; Planaria possesses high regeneration capacity; examples: Taenia (Tapeworm) and Fasciola (Liver fluke).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Aschelminthes (roundworms): circular in cross-section, bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate, complete alimentary canal with a well-developed muscular pharynx, dioecious (females often longer than males) with internal fertilisation; examples: Ascaris (Roundworm), Wuchereria (Filaria worm) and Ancylostoma (Hookworm).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Annelida: metamerically segmented coelomates with longitudinal and circular muscles, closed circulatory system, nephridia for osmoregulation and excretion, and paired ganglia connected to a double ventral nerve cord; Nereis is aquatic, possesses lateral appendages called parapodia for swimming, and is dioecious, whereas earthworms (Pheretima) and leeches (Hirudinaria) are monoecious.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Arthropoda: largest phylum of Animalia (over two-thirds of all named species), chitinous exoskeleton, body divisible into head, thorax and abdomen, jointed appendages, open circulatory system, respiratory organs (gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheal system), sensory organs (antennae, compound and simple eyes, statocysts), and excretion via malpighian tubules.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Examples of Arthropoda: Economically important—Apis (Honey bee), Bombyx (Silkworm), Laccifer (Lac insect); Vectors—Anopheles, Culex, Aedes (Mosquitoes); Gregarious pest—Locusta (Locust); Living fossil—Limulus (King crab).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Mollusca: second largest animal phylum; unsegmented body covered by a calcareous shell with distinct head, muscular foot and visceral hump; feather-like gills in the mantle cavity have respiratory and excretory functions, and mouth contains a file-like rasping organ for feeding called radula.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
Examples of Mollusca: Pila (Apple snail), Pinctada (Pearl oyster), Sepia (Cuttlefish), Loligo (Squid), Octopus (Devil fish), Aplysia (Sea-hare), Dentalium (Tusk shell) and Chaetopleura (Chiton).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Echinodermata: spiny-bodied marine animals with endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles; adults are radially symmetrical while larvae are bilaterally symmetrical; distinctive water vascular system helps in locomotion, capture/transport of food and respiration; excretory system is absent; examples: Asterias (Star fish), Echinus (Sea urchin), Antedon (Sea lily), Cucumaria (Sea cucumber) and Ophiura (Brittle star).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Phylum Hemichordata: worm-like marine animals with body composed of anterior proboscis, collar and long trunk; have a rudimentary structure in the collar region called stomochord (similar to notochord), open circulatory system, gill respiration, and proboscis gland as excretory organ; examples: Balanoglossus and Saccoglossus.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
Phylum Chordata characteristics: presence of notochord, dorsal hollow single central nervous system, paired pharyngeal gill slits, ventral heart, and post-anal tail.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Protochordates (exclusively marine): Subphylum Urochordata (Tunicata) has notochord only in larval tail (e.g., Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum); Subphylum Cephalochordata has notochord extending from head to tail and persistent throughout life (e.g., Branchiostoma / Amphioxus or Lancelet).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Class Cyclostomata (jawless vertebrates, Agnatha): ectoparasites on fishes, 6–15 pairs of gill slits, sucking and circular mouth without jaws, devoid of scales and paired fins, cartilaginous cranium and vertebral column, marine but migrate to fresh water for spawning and die within a few days; examples: Petromyzon (Lamprey) and Myxine (Hagfish).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Class Osteichthyes (bony fishes): terminal mouth, 4 pairs of gills covered by an operculum on each side, cycloid/ctenoid scales, air bladder present for buoyancy, external fertilisation, mostly oviparous; examples: Marine—Exocoetus (Flying fish), Hippocampus (Sea horse); Freshwater—Labeo (Rohu), Catla (Katla), Clarias (Magur); Aquarium—Betta (Fighting fish), Pterophyllum (Angel fish).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Class Amphibia: moist skin without scales, tympanum represents ear, alimentary canal, urinary and reproductive tracts open into a common cloaca, respiration by gills, lungs and skin, 3-chambered heart (2 auricles, 1 ventricle), cold-blooded; examples: Bufo (Toad), Rana (Frog), Hyla (Tree frog), Salamandra (Salamander), Ichthyophis (Limbless amphibia).
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

Class Mammalia: unique mammary glands, hair on skin, external ears (pinnae), heterodont teeth, 4-chambered heart, homoiothermous; Oviparous mammal: Ornithorhynchus (Platypus); Viviparous: Macropus (Kangaroo), Pteropus (Flying fox), Camelus, Macaca, Rattus, Canis, Felis, Elephas, Equus, Delphinus (Common dolphin), Balaenoptera (Blue whale), Panthera tigris, Panthera leo.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
As over a million species of animals have been described till now, the need for classification becomes all the more important.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
The classification also helps in assigning a systematic position to newly described species.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
Though all members of Animalia are multicellular, all of them do not exhibit the same pattern of organisation of cells.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
For example, in sponges, the cells are arranged as loose cell aggregates, i.e., they exhibit cellular level of organisation.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
Some division of labour (activities) occur among the cells.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom
In coelenterates, the arrangement of cells is more complex.
XI Ch 4: Animal Kingdom

A still higher level of organisation, i.e., organ level is exhibited by members of Platyhelminthes and other higher phyla where tissues are grouped together to form organs, each specialised for a particular function.
XI Ch 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants

Katherine Esau (1898–1997) reported in her early publications that the curly top virus spreads through a plant via the food-conducting or phloem tissue; her 1960 book 'The Anatomy of Seed Plants' was referred to as Webster's of plant biology.
XI Ch 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants

In dicotyledonous plants, direct elongation of the radicle leads to the primary root and its lateral branches (tap root system, e.g., mustard); in monocotyledons, the short-lived primary root is replaced by roots originating from the base of the stem (fibrous root system, e.g., wheat).
XI Ch 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants
Roots arising from parts of the plant other than the radicle are called adventitious roots, e.g., grass, Monstera and the banyan tree.
XI Ch 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants

Regions of the root from apex upwards: Root cap (thimble-like protective structure) → Region of meristematic activity (small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm) → Region of elongation (responsible for growth in length) → Region of maturation (epidermal cells form delicate thread-like root hairs).
XI Ch 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants
The stem develops from the plumule of the embryo of a germinating seed and bears nodes (where leaves are borne) and internodes (portions between two nodes).
XI Ch 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants
In monocotyledons, the leaf base expands into a sheath covering the stem partially or wholly; in some leguminous plants, the leaf base may become swollen and is called the pulvinus.
XI Ch 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants
Reticulate venation (veinlets form a network) is characteristic of dicotyledons, while parallel venation (veins run parallel within a lamina) is characteristic of most monocotyledons.
XI Ch 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants

In a pinnately compound leaf, a number of leaflets are present on a common axis, the rachis (representing the midrib), as in neem; in palmately compound leaves, leaflets are attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole, as in silk cotton.
XI Ch 5: Morphology of Flowering Plants

Isobilateral (monocot) leaf anatomy: Stomata are present on both surfaces of the epidermis, mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma, and certain adaxial epidermal cells along veins in grasses are modified into large, empty, colourless bulliform cells that curl leaves inwards during water stress.

Partial pressures (in mm Hg) of O2 vs CO2: Atmospheric air (pO2 = 159, pCO2 = 0.3), Alveoli (pO2 = 104, pCO2 = 40), Deoxygenated blood (pO2 = 40, pCO2 = 45), Oxygenated blood (pO2 = 95, pCO2 = 40), and Tissues (pO2 = 40, pCO2 = 45).

The solubility of CO2 is 20–25 times higher than that of O2; the diffusion membrane (total thickness much less than a millimetre) consists of three major layers: thin squamous epithelium of alveoli, endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and the basement substance in between them.

Each haemoglobin molecule can carry a maximum of 4 molecules of O2, forming a sigmoid Oxygen dissociation curve; high pO2, low pCO2, lesser H+ concentration and lower temperature in alveoli favour oxyhaemoglobin formation, while low pO2, high pCO2, high H+ and higher temperature in tissues favour dissociation.

Blood consists of plasma (55%) and formed elements (45%); plasma is 90–92% water and 6– 8% proteins: fibrinogen (for clotting/coagulation), globulins (defense mechanisms), and albumins (osmotic balance); plasma without clotting factors is called serum.
XI Ch 15: Body Fluids and Circulation

Erythrocytes (RBCs): 5 to 5.5 million mm-3 of blood in a healthy adult man, formed in red bone marrow, devoid of nucleus in most mammals and biconcave in shape, contain 12–16 gms of haemoglobin per 100 ml of blood, average life span of 120 days, and destroyed in the spleen (graveyard of RBCs).

Platelets (thrombocytes): cell fragments produced from megakaryocytes in bone marrow, numbering 1,50,000–3,50,000 mm-3 of blood, involved in blood coagulation.

Rh antigen (present in 80% of humans) incompatibility between an Rh-ve pregnant mother and an Rh+ve foetus can cause erythroblastosis foetalis (severe anaemia and jaundice) in subsequent pregnancies, prevented by administering anti-Rh antibodies to the mother immediately after the delivery of the first child.

In blood coagulation, thrombokinase converts inactive prothrombin into thrombin, which converts inactive fibrinogen into a network of fibrin threads; calcium ions (Ca2+) play a very important role in clotting.

Circulatory pathways: Open circulatory system in arthropods and molluscs; closed circulatory system in annelids and chordates; 2-chambered heart (single circulation) in fishes; 3-chambered heart (incomplete double circulation) in amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles); 4-chambered heart (complete double circulation) in crocodiles, birds and mammals.

Human heart is mesodermally derived, protected by double-walled pericardium; tricuspid valve guards the right atrio-ventricular opening, bicuspid (mitral) valve guards the left atrio-ventricular opening, and semilunar valves guard the pulmonary artery and aorta openings.

The sino-atrial node (SAN) in the right upper corner of the right atrium generates the maximum action potentials (70–75 min-1, average 72 beats min-1) and is called the pacemaker; the atrio- ventricular node (AVN) is in the lower left corner of the right atrium, giving rise to the AV bundle (bundle of His) and Purkinje fibres.

Cardiac cycle duration is 0.8 seconds: joint diastole → atrial systole (increases ventricular blood flow by 30%) → ventricular systole (first heart sound 'lub' due to closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves) → ventricular diastole (second heart sound 'dub' due to closure of semilunar valves).

Stroke volume is the volume of blood pumped out by each ventricle during a cardiac cycle (≈70 mL); Cardiac output = Stroke volume × Heart rate = 5000 mL or 5 litres per minute.

In a standard Electrocardiogram (ECG), the P-wave represents electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, the QRS complex represents depolarisation of the ventricles, and the T- wave represents repolarisation of the ventricles (end of T-wave marks the end of systole).

Arteries and veins have three layers: inner tunica intima (squamous endothelium), middle tunica media (smooth muscle and elastic fibres, comparatively thin in veins), and outer tunica externa (fibrous connective tissue with collagen fibres); the hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before systemic circulation.

Circulatory disorders: Hypertension (blood pressure >= 140/90 mm Hg vs normal 120/80 mm Hg), Coronary Artery Disease / atherosclerosis (lumen narrowing due to deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue), Angina pectoris (acute chest pain due to insufficient oxygen to heart muscle), and Heart failure (heart not pumping blood effectively enough).

Ammonia is the most toxic nitrogenous waste and requires large amounts of water (Ammonotelism: many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects); Urea is lesser toxic (Ureotelism: mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes); Uric acid is least toxic and excreted as pellet or paste with minimum water loss (Uricotelism: reptiles, birds, land snails and insects).
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination

Excretory structures in animals: Protonephridia or flame cells (Platyhelminthes like Planaria, rotifers, some annelids, and cephalochordate Amphioxus), Nephridia (earthworms and other annelids), Malpighian tubules (most insects including cockroaches), and Antennal glands or green glands (crustaceans like prawns).
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination

Human kidneys are situated between the levels of the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebra, measuring 10–12 cm in length, 5–7 cm in width, 2–3 cm in thickness, and weighing 120–170 g; the cortex extends between medullary pyramids as renal columns called Columns of Bertini.
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination

Each kidney has nearly one million nephrons consisting of the glomerulus (tuft of capillaries formed by afferent arteriole) and renal tubule (Bowman's capsule, PCT, Henle's loop, DCT); glomerulus + Bowman's capsule = Malpighian body or renal corpuscle.
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination

Cortical nephrons (majority of nephrons) have a short loop of Henle and absent or highly reduced vasa recta, whereas juxtamedullary nephrons have a very long loop of Henle running deep into the medulla with well-developed vasa recta.
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination

Glomerular filtration (ultrafiltration) filters 1100–1200 ml of blood per minute (≈1/5th of cardiac output) through 3 layers (endothelium of glomerular vessels, basement membrane, and podocytes of Bowman's capsule with filtration slits); Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is 125 ml/minute or 180 litres/day, while urine output is 1–1.5 litres/day (≈99% reabsorbed).
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination
Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium and reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients and 70–80% of electrolytes and water.
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination

The descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes (concentrating the filtrate), whereas the ascending limb is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes (diluting the filtrate); DCT performs conditional reabsorption of Na+ and water.
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination

The counter current mechanism between the two limbs of Henle's loop and vasa recta maintains an osmolarity gradient from 300 mOsmolL-1 in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmolL-1 in the inner medulla (caused mainly by NaCl and urea), concentrating human urine nearly four times.
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination

Human urine is slightly acidic (pH 6.0), excreting 25–30 gm of urea per day; presence of glucose (Glycosuria) and ketone bodies (Ketonuria) in urine are indicative of diabetes mellitus; lungs remove 200 mL/minute of CO2.
XI Ch 16: Excretory Products and their Elimination

Excretory disorders: Uremia (accumulation of urea in blood, treated by haemodialysis using a cellophane tube and heparin/anti-heparin), Renal calculi (insoluble mass of crystallised salts like oxalates), and Glomerulonephritis (inflammation of glomeruli).

Animals accumulate ammonia, urea, uric acid, carbon dioxide, water and ions like Na+ , K+ , Cl– , phosphate, sulphate, etc., either by metabolic activities or by other means like excess ingestion.

XI Ch 17: Locomotion and Movement

Three main types of movements in human cells: amoeboid (macrophages and leucocytes, involving pseudopodia and microfilaments), ciliary (trachea for removing dust, female reproductive tract for passage of ova), and muscular (limbs, jaws, tongue); flagellar movement helps in swimming of spermatozoa, water current in sponges, and locomotion in Euglena.
XI Ch 17: Locomotion and Movement

Muscle is a specialised tissue of mesodermal origin contributing 40–50% of adult human body weight: Skeletal muscles are striated and voluntary; Visceral (smooth) muscles are non-striated (smooth) and involuntary; Cardiac muscles are striated, branched and involuntary.

Each skeletal muscle consists of muscle bundles (fascicles) held together by a collagenous connective tissue layer called fascia; each muscle fibre is a syncytium lined by sarcolemma enclosing sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum (storehouse of Ca2+), and myofibrils.

Each thin (actin) filament consists of two helically wound 'F' (filamentous) actins (polymers of monomeric 'G' globular actins), two filaments of tropomyosin, and a complex protein Troponin (whose subunit masks active binding sites for myosin in the resting state).
XI Ch 17: Locomotion and Movement

Each thick (myosin) filament is a polymer of meromyosins, each having a globular head with a short arm (heavy meromyosin, HMM, which projects outwards as a cross arm and has ATPase activity and binding sites for ATP and actin) and a tail (light meromyosin, LMM).
XI Ch 17: Locomotion and Movement

According to the sliding filament theory, acetylcholine released at the neuromuscular junction (motor-end plate) triggers Ca2+ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum, which binds to troponin, exposing active sites on actin for myosin cross-bridge formation; during contraction, the 'I' bands and 'H' zone get reduced while the 'A' bands retain their length.

Red muscle fibres have high myoglobin content, plenty of mitochondria, and carry out aerobic respiration (aerobic muscles), whereas White muscle fibres have very less myoglobin, few mitochondria, high sarcoplasmic reticulum, and depend on anaerobic processes.

Human skeleton has 206 bones divided into Axial skeleton (80 bones) and Appendicular skeleton (126 bones); the skull has 22 bones (8 cranial and 14 facial), a single U-shaped hyoid bone at the base of the buccal cavity, 6 ear ossicles (Malleus, Incus and Stapes in each middle ear), and two occipital condyles (dicondylic skull).

Vertebral column has 26 serially arranged vertebrae: Cervical (7, first vertebra is atlas), Thoracic (12), Lumbar (5), Sacral (1-fused) and Coccygeal (1-fused); sternum is a flat bone on the ventral midline of thorax.
XI Ch 17: Locomotion and Movement

There are 12 pairs of bicephalic ribs: first 7 pairs are true ribs (attached dorsally to thoracic vertebrae and ventrally to sternum via hyaline cartilage), 8th, 9th and 10th pairs are vertebrochondral (false) ribs (join the 7th rib), and 11th and 12th pairs are floating ribs (not connected ventrally).
XI Ch 17: Locomotion and Movement

Each forelimb (30 bones) has humerus (1), radius (1), ulna (1), carpals (8 wrist bones), metacarpals (5 palm bones), and phalanges (14 digits); each hindlimb (30 bones) has femur (1, longest bone), patella (1, cup-shaped knee cap), tibia (1), fibula (1), tarsals (7 ankle bones), metatarsals (5), and phalanges (14).
XI Ch 17: Locomotion and Movement

Pectoral girdle has clavicle (collar bone) and scapula (large triangular flat bone between 2nd and 7th ribs with spine, acromion process and glenoid cavity for humerus); Pelvic girdle has two coxal bones (each formed by fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis with acetabulum cavity) meeting ventrally at the pubic symphysis (fibrous cartilage).
XI Ch 17: Locomotion and Movement

Joints: Fibrous joints (immovable, e.g., sutures between flat skull bones), Cartilaginous joints (limited movement, e.g., between adjacent vertebrae and pubic symphysis), and Synovial joints (fluid- filled synovial cavity: ball and socket between humerus and pectoral girdle, hinge at knee joint, pivot between atlas and axis, gliding between carpals, and saddle between carpal and metacarpal of thumb).

Human neural system is divided into Central Neural System (CNS: brain and spinal cord) and Peripheral Neural System (PNS: afferent and efferent nerve fibres); PNS is divided into somatic neural system (CNS to skeletal muscles) and autonomic neural system (CNS to involuntary organs/smooth muscles, further classified into sympathetic and parasympathetic).

Nissl's granules are present in the cell body (soma) and dendrites of a neuron, but absent in the axon.

Based on number of axon and dendrites, neurons are: Multipolar (one axon and two or more dendrites, found in cerebral cortex), Bipolar (one axon and one dendrite, found in retina of eye), and Unipolar (cell body with one axon only, found usually in embryonic stage).

Myelinated nerve fibres are enveloped with Schwann cells forming a myelin sheath with gaps called nodes of Ranvier (found in spinal and cranial nerves); unmyelinated nerve fibres are enclosed by a Schwann cell that does not form a myelin sheath (found in autonomous and somatic neural systems).

In a resting neuron, the axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to K+ and nearly impermeable to Na+ and negatively charged axoplasmic proteins; the sodium-potassium pump actively transports 3 Na+ outwards for 2 K+ into the cell, maintaining a positively charged outer surface and negatively charged inner surface (resting potential).

When a stimulus is applied, rapid influx of Na+ reverses polarity (depolarisation / action potential), followed quickly by K+ diffusion outside (repolarisation) to restore the resting potential.

Impulse transmission across electrical synapses (where pre- and post-synaptic membranes are in very close proximity) is always faster than across chemical synapses (where neurotransmitters are released into the fluid-filled synaptic cleft to bind post-synaptic receptors).

Human brain is covered by three cranial meninges: outer dura mater, very thin middle arachnoid, and inner pia mater (in contact with brain tissue).

The inner parts of cerebral hemispheres and associated deep structures like amygdala and hippocampus form the limbic lobe or limbic system, which along with the hypothalamus regulates sexual behaviour, emotional reactions (excitement, pleasure, rage, fear) and motivation.

Midbrain is located between thalamus/hypothalamus and pons; a canal called the cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain, and its dorsal portion consists of four round swellings (lobes) called corpora quadrigemina.

Hindbrain comprises pons (fibre tracts interconnecting brain regions), cerebellum (very convoluted surface to provide additional space for neurons), and medulla oblongata (controls respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions); the brain stem is made up of midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata.
XI Ch 18: Neural Control and Coordination
Coordination is the process through which two or more organs interact and complement the functions of one another.
XI Ch 18: Neural Control and Coordination
For example, when we do physical exercises, the energy demand is increased for maintaining an increased muscular activity.
XI Ch 18: Neural Control and Coordination
The increased supply of oxygen necessitates an increase in the rate of respiration, heart beat and increased blood flow via blood vessels.
XI Ch 18: Neural Control and Coordination
When physical exercise is stopped, the activities of nerves, lungs, heart and kidney gradually return to their normal conditions.
XI Ch 18: Neural Control and Coordination
In our body the neural system and the endocrine system jointly coordinate and integrate all the activities of the organs so that they function in a synchronised fashion.

The neural system provides an organised network of point-to-point connections for a quick coordination.

The endocrine system provides chemical integration through hormones.

The neural organisation is very simple in lower invertebrates.

For example, in Hydra it is composed of a network of neurons.

The neural system is better organised in insects, where a brain is present along with a number of ganglia and neural tissues.

The vertebrates have a more developed neural system.

The PNS comprises of all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS (brain and spinal cord).
XI Ch 18: Neural Control and Coordination
The cell body contains cytoplasm with typical cell organelles and certain granular bodies called Nissl’s granules.

Short fibres which branch repeatedly and project out of the cell body also contain Nissl’s granules and are called dendrites.

The axon is a long fibre, the distal end of which is branched.
XI Ch 18: Neural Control and Coordination
Each branch terminates as a bulb-like structure called synaptic knob which possess synaptic vesicles containing chemicals called neurotransmitters.
XI Ch 18: Neural Control and Coordination
The axons transmit nerve impulses away from the cell body to a synapse or to a neuro- muscular junction.
XI Ch 18: Neural Control and Coordination
The gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths are called nodes of Ranvier.

Nerve Impulse Neurons are excitable cells because their membranes are in a polarised state.

Different types of ion channels are present on the neural membrane.

In contrast, the fluid outside the axon contains a low concentration of K + , a high concentration of Na+ and thus form a concentration gradient.

The electrical potential difference across the resting plasma membrane is called as the resting potential.

The polarity of the membrane at the site A is thus reversed and hence depolarised.

At sites immediately ahead, the axon (e.g., site B) membrane has a positive charge on the outer surface and a negative charge on its inner surface.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals which act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Hypothalamus (basal part of diencephalon) contains neurosecretory nuclei producing releasing hormones (e.g., GnRH) and inhibiting hormones (e.g., somatostatin) that reach the anterior pituitary via a portal circulatory system, while the posterior pituitary is under direct neural regulation.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Pituitary gland is located in a bony cavity called sella tursica and divided into adenohypophysis (pars distalis and pars intermedia) and neurohypophysis (pars nervosa); pars distalis produces GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH, while pars intermedia secretes only MSH.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) stores and releases two hormones actually synthesised by the hypothalamus: oxytocin (stimulates vigorous uterine contraction at childbirth and milk ejection) and vasopressin / ADH (stimulates water and electrolyte resorption by distal tubules; deficiency causes Diabetes Insipidus).
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Over-secretion of GH in childhood causes gigantism, low secretion causes pituitary dwarfism, and excess secretion of GH in adults (especially middle age) causes severe facial disfigurement called Acromegaly.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

In males, LH stimulates synthesis and secretion of androgens from testis while FSH and androgens regulate spermatogenesis; in females, LH induces ovulation of Graafian follicles and maintains corpus luteum, while FSH stimulates growth and development of ovarian follicles.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Pineal gland (on dorsal side of forebrain) secretes melatonin, which regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of the body (sleep-wake cycle, body temperature) and influences metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle and defense capability.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Thyroid gland consists of two lobes connected by a thin flap of connective tissue called isthmus; follicular cells synthesise tetraiodothyronine/thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) requiring iodine, while stromal/parafollicular tissue secretes a protein hormone thyrocalcitonin (TCT) which decreases blood Ca2+ levels.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Iodine deficiency causes hypothyroidism and goitre; hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes cretinism (stunted growth, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin, deaf-mutism), while hyperthyroidism causes Exophthalmic goitre or Graves' disease (enlargement of thyroid, protrusion of eyeballs, increased BMR, weight loss).
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Four parathyroid glands on the back side of the thyroid gland secrete a peptide hormone, parathyroid hormone (PTH), which is a hypercalcemic hormone that increases blood Ca2+ levels by bone resorption/demineralisation, renal Ca2+ reabsorption, and Ca2+ absorption from digested food.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Thymus gland (lobular structure between lungs behind sternum on ventral side of aorta) secretes peptide hormones called thymosins that differentiate T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity) and promote antibody production (humoral immunity); thymus degenerates in old individuals, weakening immune responses.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines—adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine)—known as emergency hormones or hormones of Fight or Flight, which increase alertness, pupillary dilation, piloerection, sweating, heart rate, and glycogenolysis.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Adrenal cortex has three layers: inner zona reticularis, middle zona fasciculata, and outer zona glomerulosa; underproduction of hormones by the adrenal cortex alters carbohydrate metabolism causing acute weakness and fatigue called Addison's disease.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Cortisol (main glucocorticoid) stimulates gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, proteolysis and RBC production, maintains cardiovascular and kidney functions, produces anti-inflammatory reactions and suppresses immune response; Aldosterone (main mineralocorticoid) stimulates reabsorption of Na+ and water and excretion of K+ and phosphate ions at renal tubules.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Endocrine pancreas has 1 to 2 million Islets of Langerhans (1–2% of pancreatic tissue): α-cells secrete glucagon (hyperglycemic peptide hormone stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis), and β-cells secrete insulin (hypoglycemic peptide hormone enhancing cellular glucose uptake and glycogenesis); prolonged hyperglycemia causes diabetes mellitus.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Leydig cells (interstitial cells) in intertubular spaces of testis produce androgens (mainly testosterone), which regulate male accessory sex organs, spermatogenesis, male sexual behaviour (libido), and anabolic effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Growing ovarian follicles synthesise estrogen, while the ruptured follicle after ovulation forms the corpus luteum which secretes mainly progesterone (supports pregnancy and stimulates mammary alveoli formation and milk secretion).
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Hormones of non-endocrine tissues: Atrial wall of heart secretes atrial natriuretic factor (ANF, causes vasodilation and decreases blood pressure); juxtaglomerular cells of kidney produce erythropoietin (stimulates erythropoiesis/RBC formation).
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Gastrointestinal tract peptide hormones: Gastrin (stimulates gastric glands to secrete HCl and pepsinogen), Secretin (acts on exocrine pancreas to stimulate secretion of water and bicarbonate ions), Cholecystokinin / CCK (acts on both pancreas and gall bladder to stimulate secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice), and Gastric Inhibitory Peptide / GIP (inhibits gastric secretion and motility).
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
The neural coordination is fast but short-lived.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
As the nerve fibres do not innervate all cells of the body and the cellular functions need to be continuously regulated; a special kind of coordination and integration has to be provided.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
The neural system and the endocrine system jointly coordinate and regulate the physiological functions in the body.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
Endocrine glands lack ducts and are hence, called ductless glands.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
The new definition covers a number of new molecules in addition to the hormones secreted by the organised endocrine glands.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
Invertebrates possess very simple endocrine systems with few hormones whereas a large number of chemicals act as hormones and provide coordination in the vertebrates.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Glands and Hormones Endocrine System Heart, Kidney and Gastrointestinal Tract Hormone Action The endocrine glands and hormone producing diffused tissues/cells located in different parts of our body constitute the endocrine system.

In addition to these, some other organs, e.g., gastrointestinal tract, liver, kidney, heart also produce hormones.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
For example a hypothalamic hormone called Gonadotrophin releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulates the pituitary synthesis and release of gonadotrophins.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
Adenohypophysis consists of two portions, pars distalis and pars intermedia.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
Over-secretion of GH stimulates abnormal growth of the body leading to gigantism and low secretion of GH results in stunted growth resulting in pituitary dwarfism.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration

Excess secretion of growth hormone in adults especially in middle age can result in severe disfigurement (especially of the face) called Acromegaly, which may lead to serious complications, and premature death if unchecked.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
The disease is hard to diagnose in the early stages and often goes undetected for many years, until changes in external features become noticeable.
XI Ch 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
Prolactin regulates the growth of the mammary glands and formation of milk in them.

TSH stimulates the synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland.

ACTH stimulates the synthesis and secretion of steroid hormones called glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex.

[NCERT p. 26]

chem: XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Matter Classification: Pure substances have fixed composition (elements, compounds); mixtures have variable composition (homogeneous solutions or heterogeneous). ▸ Pure: Fixed ratio; Mixture: Variable ratio
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

SI Base Units in Chemistry: Seven SI base units include metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol, 6.022×10^23 entities), and candela (cd). ▸ 1 mol = 6.02214076 × 10^23 elementary entities
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Mass vs Weight & Volume Conversions: Mass is constant matter content (SI unit kg), while weight W = mg varies with gravity; 1 L = 1 dm^3 = 1000 cm^3 = 10^-3 m^3. ▸ 1 m^3 = 10^3 L = 10^6 cm^3 (mL)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Temperature Scale Conversions: Kelvin temperature relates to Celsius as T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15, and Fahrenheit relates to Celsius as °F = (9/5)°C + 32. ▸ °F = 1.8(°C) + 32; −40°C = −40°F
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Significant Figures Rules: All non-zero digits and captive zeros are significant. ▸ 0.002050 has 4 sig. figs; 2.50 × 10^3 has 3 sig. figs
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Precision vs Accuracy: Precision reflects closeness among repeated measurements of the same quantity. ▸ Small random spread ⇒ High precision; Zero systematic bias ⇒ High accuracy
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Rounding Off Rules in Calculations: In multiplication/division, keep as many significant figures as the factor with fewest sig. figs. ▸ Digit 5 rule: Preceding odd digit rounds up (+1), even stays unchanged
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier, 1789): In all physical and chemical changes (ignoring nuclear mass defect), the total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants. ▸ ∑ m_reactants = ∑ m_products
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Law of Definite Proportions (Proust, 1799): A given chemical compound always contains the exact same constituent elements combined together in the same fixed proportion. ▸ Pure H2O always has m(H) : m(O) = 1 : 8 by mass
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Law of Multiple Proportions (Dalton, 1803): When two elements combine to form more than one compound. ▸ CO (12:16) vs CO2 (12:32) ⇒ Oxygen ratio = 16 : 32 = 1 : 2
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Gay-Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes (1808): When gases combine or are produced in a chemical rxn at the same temp. ▸ H2(1 vol) + Cl2(1 vol) → 2HCl(2 vol) ⇒ Ratio 1 : 1 : 2
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Avogadro's Law (1811): Equal volumes of all ideal gases maintained at the same temperature and pressure contain an equal number of molecules (V ∝ n at constant P, T). ▸ V1 / n1 = V2 / n2 (At constant T and P)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Dalton's Atomic Theory Limitations: Dalton's theory explained the laws of chemical combination by mass but failed to explain Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes, isotopes. ▸ Atoms are divisible into e^−, p^+, and n^0
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Atomic Mass Unit (1 u or 1 Da): One unified atomic mass unit (1 u) is defined as exactly 1/12th of the mass of one single unbound neutral carbon-12 (12C) atom. ▸ 1 u = 1 / N_A g = 1.66056 × 10^−24 g = 1.66056 × 10^−27 kg
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Average Atomic Mass of Isotopic Mixtures: For an element existing as isotopes with relative fractional abundances x_i and isotopic masses A_i. ▸ A_avg = ∑ (p_i A_i) / 100 (For Cl: 0.75×35 + 0.25×37 = 35.5 u)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Boron and Bromine Average Atomic Masses: Natural Boron has average atomic mass 10.8 u; Bromine has average atomic mass 80.0 u. ▸ Copper (69.1% 63Cu, 30.9% 65Cu) ⇒ A_avg = 63.55 u
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Molecular Mass vs Formula Mass: Molecular mass is the sum of atomic masses in a discrete molecule; ionic solids without discrete molecules use formula mass. ▸ Formula mass of NaCl = 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5 u
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Mole Concept and Avogadro Constant (N_A): One mole of any substance contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in exactly 12 g. ▸ n = W(g) / M_0 = N / N_A = V_STP(L) / 22.4 (or 22.7 L at 1 bar)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Molar Volume of Ideal Gas at STP vs NTP: At modern IUPAC STP, 1 mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.7 L; at old STP/NTP, it occupies 22.4 L. ▸ V_m(273.15 K, 1 bar) = 22.7 L mol^−1; V_m(1 atm) = 22.4 L mol^−1
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Number of Electrons, Protons, and Neutrons in 1 Mole: For a species of molar mass M_0 containing k e⁻ per molecule, mass W contains (W/M_0) × k × N_A particles. ▸ 1.6 g CH4 (0.1 mol) contains 0.1 × 10 × N_A = N_A e⁻
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Charge of 1 Mole of Electrons: The magnitude of electric charge carried by 1 mole of e⁻ equals N_A × e = 96,485 C mol^−1 ≈ 96,500 C (1 Faraday). ▸ Q = n × z × F (where F = N_A e ≈ 96,500 C mol^−1)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Mass of a Single Atom or Molecule: The actual mass in grams of 1 single atom of an element of atomic mass A is A/N_A g; 1 gram-atom means 1 mole of atoms. ▸ Mass of 1 H2O molecule = 18 / (6.022 × 10^23) = 2.99 × 10^−23 g
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Atomicity and Total Atoms in Polyatomic Samples: Total no. of atoms in n moles of a molecule of atomicity a is n × a × N_A. ▸ Equal masses of O2 and O3 contain identical total no. of O atoms!
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Vapour Density (VD) and Molar Mass of a Gas: Vapour density of a gas is the ratio of the mass of a volume V of the gas to the mass of an equal volume V of H2 gas at the same T. ▸ Molar Mass M_0 = 2 × Vapour Density (VD)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Average Molar Mass of a Gaseous Mixture: For a non-reacting mixture of gases with moles n_i and molar masses M_i. ▸ M_mix = (n1 M1 + n2 M2 + ...) / (n1 + n2 + ...) = ∑ (x_i M_i)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Percentage Composition by Mass: The mass percentage of an element in a compound is the total mass of that element in 1 mole of the compound divided. ▸ Mass % of element = [(No. of atoms × Atomic mass) / Molar mass] × 100%
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Minimum Molar Mass of a Biomolecule: If a macromolecule contains p% by mass of an element of atomic mass. ▸ M_min = (A × 100) / p (If k atoms are present: M = k × M_min)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Empirical Formula vs Molecular Formula: Empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. ▸ Molecular Formula = n × (Empirical Formula), where n = M_molecular / M_empirical
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Compounds Sharing Identical Empirical Formulas: Acetylene (C2H2) and benzene (C6H6) share empirical formula CH. ▸ All alkenes (CnH2n) and cycloalkanes share empirical formula CH2 (85.7% C)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Combustion Analysis: When mass W of an organic compound is completely burnt to yield m_CO2 of CO2 and m_H2O of H2O, the masses of C and H come from fractions 12/44 and 2/18. ▸ % C = (12 / 44)(m_CO2 / W) × 100
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Eudiometry (Hydrocarbon Combustion Equation): Complete combustion of 1 mole of hydrocarbon C_xH_y consumes moles of O2 and produces x moles of CO2 and (y/2) moles. ▸ CxHy(g) + (x + y/4)O2(g) → x CO2(g) + (y/2) H2O(l)
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

KOH and Alkaline Pyrogallol Gas Absorbents: In eudiometry, aq. KOH (or NaOH) selectively absorbs acidic gases (CO2, SO2), alkaline pyrogallol absorbs O2, and ammoniacal CuCl absorbs CO. ▸ Turpentine oil absorbs O3
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
Percentage Yield of a Chemical Reaction: Because of side rxns or incomplete conversion. ▸ % Yield = (Actual Yield / Theoretical Yield) × 100%

Percentage Purity of an Impure Ore or Sample: When an impure sample of total mass W_impure yields product corresponding to pure reactant. ▸ % Purity = (Mass of Pure Substance Reacted / Total Mass of Impure Sample) × 100%
XI Ch 1: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry

Principle of Atom Conservation (POAC): In any multi-step chemical process where all of a specific element from reactant A ends up. ▸ (Moles of A) × (Atoms of element per A) = (Moles of B) × (Atoms of element per B)

Nuclear Radius vs Mass Number Relation: The radius R of an atomic nucleus of mass number A is ∝ the cube root. ▸ R = R_0 A^(1/3) (where R_0 ≈ 1.2 to 1.33 × 10^−15 m = 1.2 to 1.33 fm)

Isotopes, Isobars, Isotones, and Isodiaphers: Isotopes have the same Z but different A (1H, 2H, 3H) ▸ Alpha decay leaves (A − 2Z) unchanged, so parent and α-daughter are ISODIAPHERS!

Electromagnetic Wave Parameters: All electromagnetic waves travel in vacuum at speed c = 3.0 × 10^8 m s^−1. ▸ c = ν λ; Wavenumber ν̄ = 1 / λ = ν / c (Unit: m^−1 or cm^−1)

Energy of 1 Mole of Photons: The total energy of 1 mole of photons of wavelength λ is called 1 Einstein of energy: E_molar = N_A h ν =. ▸ 1 Einstein = N_A h c / λ ≈ (0.1196 J·m·mol^−1) / λ(m) = [119627 / λ(nm)] kJ mol^−1

Blackbody Radiation: As a blackbody is heated, total emitted intensity grows as T^4 and the peak emission wavelength λ_max shifts toward shorter wavelengths. ▸ λ_max T = b = 2.898 × 10^−3 m K (Wien's Displacement Law)

Work Function Order of Alkali Metals: Because alkali metals have the lowest ionization enthalpies, they have the lowest work functions: Cs < K < Na < Li. ▸ Lowest work function metal = Caesium (Cs, W_0 ≈ 1.9–2.14 eV)

Bohr's Quantization of Angular Momentum: In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom. ▸ L_n = m_e v_n r_n = (n h) / (2π) = n ħ (where principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3, ...)

Velocity of Electron in n-th Bohr Orbit: The orbital speed v_n of the e⁻ in the n-th Bohr orbit of a one-e⁻ ion is ∝ Z and ∝ 1/ principal quantum number n. ▸ v_n = 2.188 × 10^6 × (Z / n) m s^−1 = (c / 137) × (Z / n)

Time Period and Frequency of Revolution in n-th Bohr Orbit: Since orbital circumference is 2πr_n ∝ n^2/Z and speed is v_n ∝ Z/ n. ▸ T_n = (1.52 × 10^−16 s) × (n^3 / Z^2) ∝ n^3 / Z^2

Kinetic, Potential, and Total Energy Ratios in a Bohr Orbit: In any circular Bohr orbit, total energy E_n is negative, kinetic energy K_n equals −E_n. ▸ K_n = −E_n; U_n = 2 E_n = −2 K_n ⇒ K_n : E_n : U_n = +1 : −1 : −2

Ritz Combination Principle for Cascading Transitions: If an e⁻ jumps from level 3 → 1 in two steps. ▸ ν_3→1 = ν_3→2 + ν_2→1; ν̄_3→1 = ν̄_3→2 + ν̄_2→1

Anomalous Pairs in Mendeleev's Periodic Table: Mendeleev prioritized chemical properties over strict atomic weight order. ▸ Anomalous mass inversions resolved by atomic number Z: (Ar, K), (Co, Ni), (Te, I), (Th, Pa)

Moseley's Modern Periodic Law (1913): Henry Moseley showed that the square root of characteristic X-ray frequency √ν is a linear function of atomic. ▸ √ν = a (Z − b) ⇒ Atomic number Z is the fundamental periodic property
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Long Form of Periodic Table: The modern IUPAC periodic table has 7 horizontal periods and 18 vertical groups. ▸ Period number = Maximum principal quantum number n of valence shell
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Number of Elements in Each of the Seven Periods: Period 1 (n=1: 1s) has 2 elements; Periods 2 and 3 (ns np) have 8 elements each. ▸ Magic numbers of elements in Periods 1 to 7: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

IUPAC Systematic Nomenclature for Elements with Z > 100: Digits 0 to 9 use roots: 0=nil, 1=un, 2=bi, 3=tri, 4=quad, 5=pent, 6=hex, 7=sept. ▸ 0=nil, 1=un, 2=bi, 3=tri, 4=quad, 5=pent, 6=hex, 7=sept, 8=oct, 9=enn + ium
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Official IUPAC Names of Superheavy Elements Z = 101 to Z = 118: 101 Mendelevium (Md), 102 Nobelium (No), 103 Lawrencium (Lr), 104 Rutherfordium (Rf), 105 Dubnium (Db), 106 Seaborgium (Sg). ▸ Z=101: Mendelevium (Md)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
p-Block Elements: p-Block spans Groups 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18; together with s-block they are called Representative or Main- Group elements. ▸ Chalcogens (Ore-forming) = Group 16 (ns^2 np^4)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
d-Block Transition Elements (Groups 3 to 12): d-Block elements have general config. ▸ Zn (Z=30), Cd (Z=48), and Hg (Z=80) have completely filled (n−1)d^10 ns^2 in both ground
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
f-Block Inner-Transition Elements: f-Block elements have general config. ▸ All 14 Lanthanoids and 14 Actinoids belong to Group 3!
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Transuranic Elements (Z > 92, Beyond Uranium): Elements with atomic number greater than Uranium do not occur naturally in significant amounts and are all synthetic. ▸ Uranium (Z = 92) is the last major natural element
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Finding Period, Block, and Group Number Directly from Atomic Number Z: Compare Z with noble gas atomic numbers: the next noble gas. ▸ Noble gas Z milestones: 2 (P1), 10 (P2), 18 (P3), 36 (P4), 54 (P5), 86 (P6), 118 (P7)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Metals, Non-Metals, and Metalloids Distribution: Over 78% of known elements are metals (left and bottom) ▸ Common Metalloids: Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Liquid Elements at or Near Room Temperature: At 25°C, only TWO elements are liquids: Mercury (Hg, Z=80, metal) and Bromine. ▸ Room-temp. liquids: Mercury (Hg, metal) and Bromine (Br, non-metal)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Covalent, Metallic, and van der Waals Radii Comparison: For any element, van der Waals radius is ALWAYS greater than metallic radius. ▸ r_van der Waals > r_metallic > r_covalent
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Periodic Trend of Atomic Radius Across a Period and Down a Group: Moving left to right across a period. ▸ Across a period (left → right): Z_eff ↑ ⇒ Atomic radius DECREASES
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Cation vs Parent Atom and Anion vs Parent Atom Size Rule: A cation is ALWAYS smaller than its parent neutral atom. ▸ For the same element: r(M^−) > r(M) > r(M^+) > r(M^2+) > r(M^3+)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Isoelectronic Species Radius Formula (r ∝ 1/Z): Among isoelectronic ions, ionic radius is ∝ 1/ nuclear charge: the ion. ▸ 10-e⁻ isoelectronic size order: C^4− > N^3− (171 pm) > O^2− (140 pm) > F^− (136 pm) > Na^+ (95 pm)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Lanthanoid Contraction and Equal Radii of 4d and 5d Transition Series: Because the 14 inner 4f e⁻ placed before the 5d series. ▸ Poor shielding of 4f e⁻ ⇒ Lanthanoid Contraction ⇒ r(Zr, 160 pm) ≈ r(Hf, 159 pm)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Gallium vs Aluminium Radius Anomaly: In Group 13, instead of increasing down the group. ▸ Group 13 atomic radius order: B (88 pm) < Ga (135 pm) < Al (143 pm) < In (167 pm) < Tl (170 pm)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Periodic Trend of First Ionization Enthalpy and Half-Filled / Full-Filled Exceptions: Across a period, IE_1 generally increases with Z_eff. ▸ Period 2 IE_1 order: Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Period 3 First Ionization Enthalpy Order: In Period 3, the exact same Group 2 > Group 13 and Group 15 > Group 16 inversions occur: Mg. ▸ Period 3 IE_1 order: Na < Al < Mg < Si < S < P < Cl < Ar (Note: Mg > Al and P > S!)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Second Ionization Enthalpy Order in Period 2: After losing 1 e⁻, X^+ adopts the electronic config. of the element just to its left. ▸ Period 2 IE_2 order: Be < C < B < N < F < O < Ne < Li
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Group 14 Ionization Enthalpy Anomaly (Pb > Sn): In Group 14, IE_1 decreases from C > Si > Ge > Sn, but increases from Tin to Lead. ▸ Group 14 IE_1 order: C > Si > Ge > Pb > Sn (Note: IE_1 of Pb > Sn!)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Highest and Lowest Ionization Enthalpy Elements in the Periodic Table: Helium (He, 1s^2) has the highest first ionization enthalpy of all elements in the periodic table. ▸ Highest IE_1 element = Helium (He)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Electron Gain Enthalpy vs Electron Affinity: Electron gain enthalpy Δ_eg H is the enthalpy change for X(g) + e^− → X^−(g) ▸ Exothermic e⁻ addition ⇒ Δ_eg H is NEGATIVE
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Second Electron Gain Enthalpy Is Always Endothermic: Adding a second e⁻ to an already negatively charged uni-negative anion [X^−(g) + e^− → X^2−(g)] faces strong. ▸ O(g) + e^− → O^−(g) (Δ_eg H_1 = −141 kJ/mol < 0)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Elements with Positive First Electron Gain Enthalpy: First e⁻ gain enthalpy is positive for: (1) all Group 18 Noble Gases, (2) Be and Mg. ▸ Positive Δ_eg H_1 elements: Noble gases, Be, Mg, and Nitrogen (N)
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Chlorine vs Fluorine and Sulphur vs Oxygen Electron Gain Enthalpy Anomaly: In Group 17, Chlorine has a MORE negative e⁻ gain enthalpy than Fluorine. ▸ Group 17 |Δ_eg H| order: Cl (−349) > F (−328) > Br (−325) > I
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Group 16 Electron Gain Enthalpy Order: In Group 16, because the tiny 2p subshell of Oxygen repels the incoming e⁻ so strongly. ▸ Group 16 |Δ_eg H| order: S (−200) > Se (−195) > Te (−190) > Po (−174) > O
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

Pauling Electronegativity Scale and Key Values: EN is the relative tendency of a bonded atom in a covalent molecule. ▸ Top EN order: F (4.0) > O (3.5) > N (3.04) ≈ Cl (3.16) > Br (2.96) > I (2.66) ≈ S (2.58) ≈ C
XI Ch 3: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
Summary of Periodic Exceptions Often Tested in NEET: Memorize these 7 classic NEET periodic inversions: (1) Radius: Ga < Al; (2) IE_1: Be > B and Mg > Al. ▸ 7 High-Yield Inversions: r(Ga) < r(Al)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Kossel-Lewis Octet Rule: Atoms combine by transfer or sharing of valence electrons to attain stable 8e⁻ configuration (2e⁻ duplet for H, Li, Be). ▸ ns²np⁶ (8 valence e⁻)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Formal Charge Formula: Difference between valence electrons of free atom (V) and electrons assigned in Lewis structure (L = lone pair e⁻, B = bonding e⁻). ▸ FC = V − L − ½B
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Formal Charge on Ozone (O₃): Central oxygen has +1, double-bonded terminal oxygen has 0, and single-bonded terminal oxygen has −1 formal charge. ▸ FC(O_central) = 6 − 2 − ½(6) = +1
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Incomplete Octet Exceptions: Electron-deficient molecules with central atom having fewer than 8 valence electrons act as strong Lewis acids. ▸ LiCl (2e⁻), BeH₂ / BeCl₂ (4e⁻), BF₃ / BCl₃ / AlCl₃ (6e⁻)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Odd-Electron Molecules: Molecules containing an odd number of valence electrons are paramagnetic due to one unpaired electron. ▸ NO (11 valence e⁻), NO₂ (17 valence e⁻), ClO₂ (19e⁻)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Expanded Octet (Hypervalent) Molecules: Elements of Period 3 and beyond use vacant 3d orbitals to accommodate more than 8 valence electrons. ▸ PF₅ (10e⁻), SF₆ (12e⁻), H₂SO₄ (12e⁻), IF₇ (14e⁻)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Electrovalent (Ionic) Bond Formation: Favored by low ionization enthalpy of metal, high negative electron gain enthalpy of non- metal, and high lattice enthalpy. ▸ M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻; X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Lattice Enthalpy (Δ_lattice H°): Energy required to completely separate one mole of solid ionic compound into gaseous constituent ions. ▸ NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g); ΔH_lat = +788 kJ mol⁻¹
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Born-Haber Cycle for Ionic Solids: Applies Hess's Law to calculate lattice enthalpy from sublimation, ionization, dissociation, e⁻ gain, and formation enthalpies. ▸ ΔH_f° = ΔH_sub + IE + ½ΔH_diss + Δ_eg H + U_lattice
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Factors Affecting Lattice Enthalpy: Directly proportional to product of ionic charges and inversely proportional to interionic distance. ▸ U_lattice ∝ (q₁ · q₂) / (r_+ + r_-)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Lattice Energy Order of Alkali Halides: For a fixed cation, lattice enthalpy decreases as halide size increases from F⁻ to I⁻. ▸ NaF > NaCl > NaBr > NaI (and LiF > NaF > KF > RbF)
