XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Solvation (Hydration) Condition for Solubility: An ionic solid dissolves in water only when hydration enthalpy exceeds its lattice enthalpy. ▸ |Δ_hyd H°| > |Δ_lattice H°| ⇒ Soluble
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Hydration Enthalpy Order of Group 1 & 2: Smaller cations have higher charge density and undergo stronger hydration in aqueous solution. ▸ Li⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺ > Rb⁺ > Cs⁺; Be²⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Sr²⁺ > Ba²⁺
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Solubility Trend of Group 2 Sulphates: Decreases down the group because hydration enthalpy drops faster than lattice enthalpy with large SO₄²⁻ anion. ▸ BeSO₄ > MgSO₄ > CaSO₄ > SrSO₄ > BaSO₄
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Fajans' Rule of Covalent Character: Polarizing power of cation increases with high charge and small size. ▸ Covalent character ∝ (q_cation / r_cation) × r_anion
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Fajans' Rule: Pseudo-Noble Gas Configuration: Cations with 18 valence electrons (ns²np⁶nd¹⁰) polarize anions more strongly than 8-electron noble gas cations. ▸ CuCl > NaCl and AgCl > KCl in covalent character
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Fajans' Rule: Anion Polarizability Order: Larger halide ions are more easily distorted, increasing covalent character and decreasing melting point. ▸ Covalent character: LiI > LiBr > LiCl > LiF
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Thermal Stability of Metal Carbonates: Increases down Group 1 and Group 2 as cation polarizing power decreases, stabilizing the polyatomic CO₃²⁻ ion. ▸ BeCO₃ < MgCO₃ < CaCO₃ < SrCO₃ < BaCO₃
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Bond Length vs Bond Multiplicity: For a given pair of atoms, bond length decreases as bond order increases from single to double to triple bond. ▸ C−C (154 pm) > C=C (134 pm) > C≡C (120 pm)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Bond Length vs s-Character: Higher percentage of s-character holds bonding electrons closer to the nucleus, shortening the C−H bond. ▸ C(sp)−H (106 pm) < C(sp²)−H (108 pm) < C(sp³)−H (109 pm)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Covalent Radius Definition: Half the internuclear distance between two identical covalently bonded atoms in the same molecule. ▸ r_cov = d_(A−A) / 2 (e.g., Cl₂: d = 198 pm ⇒ r_cov = 99 pm)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
van der Waals Radius vs Covalent Radius: Half the distance between two non-bonded atoms of adjacent molecules in solid state; always larger than covalent radius. ▸ r_vdW > r_metallic > r_covalent
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Bond Angle of Standard Hydrides: Lone pair repulsion compresses bond angles below the ideal tetrahedral angle (109.5°). ▸ CH₄ (109.5°) > NH₃ (107°) > H₂O (104.5°)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Bond Enthalpy (Bond Dissociation Energy): Energy required to break one mole of bonds of a particular type between atoms in the gaseous state. ▸ H₂(g) → 2H(g), Δ_a H° = 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Bond Enthalpy of Polyatomic Molecules: Mean bond enthalpy is the average of successive bond dissociation enthalpies in molecules like H₂O or CH₄. ▸ ΔH_mean(O−H in H₂O) = (502 + 427)/2 = 464.5 kJ mol⁻¹
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Bond Dissociation Energy of Halogens: Cl₂ has the highest bond energy; F₂ is anomalously low due to strong lone-pair–lone-pair repulsion at short bond length. ▸ Cl₂ (242) > Br₂ (193) > F₂ (158) > I₂ (151 kJ mol⁻¹)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Bond Order & Stability Relationship: Isoelectronic molecules and ions have identical bond orders; higher bond order gives higher bond energy and shorter bond length. ▸ Bond Enthalpy ∝ Bond Order ∝ 1 / Bond Length
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Isoelectronic Species with Bond Order 3: Species containing 14 total electrons possess a triple bond and bond order of 3. ▸ N₂, CO, CN⁻, NO⁺ (14e⁻ ⇒ Bond Order = 3.0)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Resonance & Canonical Structures: Resonance hybrid has lower energy and greater stability than any individual contributing canonical structure. ▸ Resonance Energy = E_(most stable canonical) − E_(hybrid)
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
C−O Bond Order in Carbonate Ion (CO₃²⁻): Three equivalent resonance structures distribute 4 shared electron pairs across 3 C−O linkages. ▸ Bond Order(CO₃²⁻) = 4 / 3 = 1.33
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Bond Orders of Polyatomic Oxyanions: Average bond order equals total no. of covalent bonds between central atom and oxygen divided by no. of peripheral oxygens. ▸ SO₄²⁻ = 6/4 = 1.5; PO₄³⁻ = 5/4 = 1.25; ClO₄⁻ = 7/4 = 1.75
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
Electric Dipole Moment (μ): Product of magnitude of charge (q) and distance of separation (r); vector points from positive to negative center (→). ▸ μ = q × r; 1 Debye (D) = 3.33564 × 10⁻³⁰ C m
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Percentage Ionic Character from Dipole Moment: Ratio of observed experimental dipole moment to theoretical dipole moment for 100% charge transfer. ▸ % Ionic Character = (μ_obs / μ_calc) × 100, where μ_calc = e × d
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Zero Dipole Moment in Symmetrical Molecules: Regular geometries with identical terminal atoms and no net lone-pair asymmetry have canceling bond dipoles. ▸ μ = 0 for CO₂, CS₂, BeF₂, BF₃, CCl₄, PCl₅, SF₆, XeF₂, XeF₄
XI Ch 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

Paramagnetic Species Among Common Oxides: Odd-electron nitrogen and chlorine oxides and dioxygen/superoxides are paramagnetic. ▸ Paramagnetic: NO, NO₂, ClO₂, ClO₃, O₂, KO₂; Diamagnetic: N₂O, N₂O₃, N₂O₄, N₂O₅
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Open, Closed, and Isolated Systems: Open exchanges both matter and energy; closed exchanges energy only. ▸ Open: Δm ≠ 0, ΔE ≠ 0; Closed: Δm = 0, ΔE ≠ 0; Isolated: Δm = 0, ΔE = 0
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

State Functions vs Path Functions: State functions depend only on initial and final states; path functions depend on the path taken. ▸ State functions: U, H, S, G, C_p, C_v; Path functions: Heat (q), Work (w)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Extensive vs Intensive Properties: Extensive properties depend on amount of matter; intensive properties are independent of amount. ▸ Ratio of two extensive properties is always intensive (e.g., ρ = m/V, C_m = C/n)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Thermodynamic Processes Classification: Isothermal (dT = 0), Isobaric (dP = 0), Isochoric (dV = 0), Adiabatic (q = 0), and Cyclic (ΔU = 0, ΔH = 0). ▸ Isothermal ideal gas: ΔU = 0, ΔH = 0; Adiabatic: q = 0 ⇒ ΔU = w
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
IUPAC Sign Convention for Heat and Work: Heat absorbed by system and work done on system are positive. ▸ q > 0 (endothermic), q < 0 (exothermic); w > 0 (compression), w < 0 (expansion)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
First Law of Thermodynamics: Energy of an isolated universe is constant; change in internal energy equals heat added plus work done on the system. ▸ ΔU = q + w
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Irreversible Pressure-Volume Work: Against a constant external pressure P_ext, mechanical work equals minus P_ext times volume change. ▸ w_irr = −P_ext ΔV = −P_ext (V₂ − V₁) (1 L atm = 101.325 J)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Free Expansion of an Ideal Gas in Vacuum: When a gas expands against vacuum, no work is done. ▸ P_ext = 0 ⇒ w = 0; Isothermal ideal gas ⇒ ΔU = 0, q = 0, ΔH = 0
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Reversible Isothermal Work of Ideal Gas: Maximum work is obtained during an infinitely slow reversible expansion at constant temperature T. ▸ w_rev = −2.303 nRT log(V₂/V₁) = −2.303 nRT log(P₁/P₂)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Comparison of Reversible vs Irreversible Work: For expansion, magnitude of reversible work exceeds irreversible work. ▸ Expansion: |w_rev| > |w_irr|; Compression: |w_irr| > |w_rev|
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Internal Energy Change at Constant Volume (q_v): In a rigid bomb calorimeter (ΔV = 0), no P-V work is performed, so heat transferred equals change in internal energy. ▸ ΔV = 0 ⇒ w = 0 ⇒ ΔU = q_v
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Enthalpy Definition & Constant-Pressure Heat: Enthalpy is defined as H = U + PV; at constant pressure, heat absorbed or evolved equals enthalpy change. ▸ H = U + PV; At constant P: ΔH = ΔU + PΔV = q_p
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Relation Between ΔH and ΔU for Gaseous Reactions: Δn_g is moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants (solids and liquids are ignored). ▸ ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Heat Capacity, Specific Heat & Molar Heat Capacity: Heat required to raise temperature by 1 K; specific heat (c) is per gram, and molar heat capacity (C_m) is per mole. ▸ q = CΔT = m·c·ΔT = n·C_m·ΔT
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

C_v and C_p Definitions: Molar heat capacity at constant volume measures (∂U/∂T)_V, while at constant pressure it measures (∂H/ ∂T)_P. ▸ ΔU = n C_v,m ΔT and ΔH = n C_p,m ΔT (always valid for ideal gases)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Mayer's Relation & Adiabatic Index (γ): For one mole of ideal gas, the difference between C_p and C_v equals the universal gas constant R. ▸ C_p,m − C_v,m = R; γ = C_p / C_v (Monoatomic: 5/3 = 1.67; Diatomic: 7/5 = 1.40)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Adiabatic Reversible Equations (Poisson's Law): For an adiabatic reversible process (q = 0) of an ideal gas, temperature, pressure, and volume obey power laws in γ. ▸ PV^γ = const; TV^(γ−1) = const; T^γ P^(1−γ) = const
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Slope of Adiabatic vs Isothermal P-V Curve: On a P-V diagram, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve at the same point by a factor of γ. ▸ (dP/dV)_adiabatic = γ · (dP/dV)_isothermal
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Bomb Calorimeter vs Coffee-Cup Calorimeter: Bomb calorimeter measures ΔU at constant V; constant-pressure calorimeter measures ΔH at atmospheric pressure. ▸ ΔU = −C_cal · ΔT / n (constant V); ΔH = q_p (constant P)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Exothermic vs Endothermic Enthalpy Diagrams: Exothermic rxns release heat; endothermic rxns absorb heat. ▸ Exothermic: Δ_r H < 0; Endothermic: Δ_r H > 0
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Kirchhoff's Equation for Enthalpy vs Temperature: Variation of rxn enthalpy with temp. ▸ (ΔH₂ − ΔH₁) / (T₂ − T₁) = ΔC_p; (ΔU₂ − ΔU₁) / (T₂ − T₁) = ΔC_v
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Joule-Thomson Effect & Inversion Temperature: Adiabatic throttling of a real gas occurs at constant enthalpy. ▸ Isenthalpic expansion: ΔH = 0; For H₂ and He at 298 K, μ_JT < 0 (warms up)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Cyclic Process Work on a P-V Indicator Diagram: In a complete cycle, ΔU = 0 and q = −w; net work equals the area enclosed by the loop. ▸ Cyclic: ∮dU = 0 ⇒ q_cycle = −w_cycle = ± Area of P-V loop
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Standard State in Chemical Thermodynamics: Purest and most stable form of a substance at 1 bar pressure and a specified temperature (usually 298.15 K). ▸ P° = 1 bar (10⁵ Pa); T = 298.15 K (25 °C)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Standard Enthalpy of Formation (Δ_f H°): Enthalpy change when 1 mole of compound is formed from its elements in their most stable reference. ▸ Δ_f H° = 0 for O₂(g), H₂(g), N₂(g), C(graphite), S₈(rhombic), Br₂(l), P(white)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Exception: Reference State of Phosphorus: Unlike carbon, less stable white phosphorus (P₄) is arbitrarily taken as Δ_f H° = 0. ▸ Δ_f H°(P_white) = 0; Δ_f H°(C_graphite) = 0; Δ_f H°(S_rhombic) = 0
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Reaction Enthalpy from Enthalpies of Formation: Standard enthalpy of any rxn equals the sum of standard enthalpies of formation of products minus reactants. ▸ Δ_r H° = ∑ ν_p Δ_f H°(products) − ∑ ν_r Δ_f H°(reactants)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Standard Enthalpy of Combustion (Δ_c H°): Enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance is completely oxidized in excess oxygen; always exothermic (Δ_c H° < 0). ▸ CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), Δ_c H° = −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Calorific Value (Fuel Value): Amount of heat produced on complete combustion of 1 gram of fuel; hydrogen (H₂) has the highest calorific value (150 kJ/g). ▸ Calorific Value = |Δ_c H°| / Molar Mass (kJ g⁻¹)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Manipulating Thermochemical Equations: Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of ΔH; multiplying stoichiometric coefficients by n multiplies ΔH by n. ▸ A → B (ΔH) ⇒ B → A (−ΔH) and nA → nB (n·ΔH)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics

Enthalpy of Atomization (Δ_a H°): Enthalpy change on breaking 1 mole of bonds completely to obtain isolated atoms in the gas phase. ▸ For metals, Δ_a H° = Δ_sub H°; For diatomics (H₂, Cl₂), Δ_a H° = Δ_bond H°
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Phase Transition Enthalpies: Enthalpy of sublimation equals the sum of enthalpy of fusion and enthalpy of vaporization at the same temperature. ▸ Δ_sub H° = Δ_fus H° + Δ_vap H°
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Trouton's Rule for Enthalpy of Vaporization: For most non-associated liquids without H-bonding. ▸ Δ_vap S = Δ_vap H / T_b ≈ 88 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (higher for H₂O due to H-bonding)
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Enthalpy of Solution (Δ_sol H°): Sum of endothermic lattice enthalpy and exothermic hydration enthalpy when 1 mole of solute dissolves in excess solvent. ▸ Δ_sol H° = Δ_lattice H° + Δ_hyd H°
XI Ch 5: Thermodynamics
Thermodynamic Efficiency of a Fuel Cell: Unlike heat engines limited by Carnot efficiency. ▸ η_max(Fuel Cell) = ΔG / ΔH = 1 − (T ΔS / ΔH)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Dynamic Nature of Chemical Equilibrium: Forward and reverse rxn rates become equal (r_f = r_b ≠ 0), while conc.s of reactants and products remain constant. ▸ At eqm: Rate_forward = Rate_backward; ΔG = 0
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Law of Mass Action & Equilibrium Constant (K_c): For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, eqm constant is the ratio of product conc.s to reactant conc.s raised to stoichiometric powers. ▸ K_c = ([C]^c [D]^d) / ([A]^a [B]^b)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Equilibrium Constant in Terms of Partial Pressures: For gaseous reactions, equilibrium constant is expressed using partial pressures (in bar or atm) of gaseous species. ▸ K_p = (P_C^c · P_D^d) / (P_A^a · P_B^b)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Relationship Between K_p and K_c: Related via the change in number of moles of gaseous species Δn_g = (n_g,products − n_g,reactants). ▸ K_p = K_c (RT)^(Δn_g), where R = 0.0831 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ or 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Characteristics of Equilibrium Constant (K): K depends ONLY on temp. and stoichiometric representation; it is independent of initial conc.s, pressure, volume, or catalyst. ▸ K = k_f / k_b (depends only on T)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Stoichiometric Manipulation of K: Reversing a rxn inverts K; multiplying by n raises K to power n; adding two rxns multiplies their K values. ▸ Reverse: K' = 1/K; Multiply by n: K' = K^n; Add Step 1 + 2: K_net = K₁ × K₂
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Heterogeneous Equilibrium Convention: Activities of pure solids and pure liquids are taken as unity (1) and omitted from K_c and K_p expressions. ▸ CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) ⇒ K_c = [CO₂(g)] and K_p = P_(CO₂)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
NH₄HS(s) Dissociation Equilibrium Pressure: For NH₄HS(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + H₂S(g), partial pressure of each gas is P_total / 2, so K_p equals P_total² / 4. ▸ K_p = P_(NH₃) · P_(H₂S) = (P/2)(P/2) = P² / 4
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
Magnitude of K and Extent of Reaction: If K_c > 10³, products predominate strongly; if K_c < 10⁻³, reactants predominate. ▸ K > 10³ ⇒ Nearly complete; K < 10⁻³ ⇒ Hardly proceeds
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Reaction Quotient vs Equilibrium Constant: Compares current concentration ratio Q_c with K_c to predict the direction of net reaction. ▸ Q_c < K_c ⇒ Forward shift; Q_c = K_c ⇒ Equilibrium; Q_c > K_c ⇒ Backward shift
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
Degree of Dissociation from Vapour Density: For A(g) ⇌ n B(g), vapour density drops from initial D to eqm d as no. of moles increases. ▸ α = (D − d) / [(n − 1) d] = (M_th − M_obs) / [(n − 1) M_obs]
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
PCl₅ Dissociation K_p Expression: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) with degree of dissociation α at total pressure P, total moles at equilibrium = 1 + α. ▸ K_p = (α² P) / (1 − α²) ≈ α² P (when α ≪ 1)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
Le Chatelier's Principle: Concentration Change: Adding a reactant or removing a product (Q < K) shifts eqm forward. ▸ Add reactant ⇒ Forward shift (K remains unchanged)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Le Chatelier's Principle: Pressure & Volume Change: Increasing total pressure shifts eqm toward the side with fewer moles of gas. ▸ Increase P (Decrease V) ⇒ Shifts toward fewer gas moles; If Δn_g = 0, no effect
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Inert Gas Addition at Constant Volume: Adding an inert gas at constant volume leaves partial pressures and molar conc.s of all species unchanged. ▸ Inert gas at Constant V ⇒ No shift in eqm for any Δn_g
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Inert Gas Addition at Constant Pressure: Adding an inert gas at constant pressure increases total volume and shifts eqm. ▸ Inert gas at Constant P ⇒ Shifts toward side with larger n_g (no shift if Δn_g = 0)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Le Chatelier's Principle: Temperature Change: Increasing temp. favors the endothermic direction; decreasing temp. favors the exothermic direction. ▸ Endothermic (ΔH > 0): T ↑ ⇒ K ↑; Exothermic (ΔH < 0): T ↑ ⇒ K ↓
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
Effect of Catalyst on Chemical Equilibrium: A catalyst lowers activation energy equally for both forward and reverse rxns. ▸ ΔE_a,f = ΔE_a,b ⇒ k_f and k_b increase by same factor ⇒ K unchanged
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Optimal Conditions for Haber Process: Since ΔH° = −92.4 kJ/mol and Δn_g = −2, high pressure, optimum temp., and Fe catalyst maximize yield. ▸ Haber Process: High P (200 bar), Optimum T (700 K), Fe catalyst
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Optimal Conditions for Contact Process: Exothermic reaction with Δn_g = −1; favored by low T (optimum 720 K for kinetics) and moderate P (≈2 bar) over V₂O₅ catalyst. ▸ Contact Process: T ≈ 720 K, P ≈ 2 bar, V₂O₅ catalyst
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
Ice ⇌ Water Physical Equilibrium (Melting Point): Since ice occupies more volume than liquid water. ▸ Ice(s, higher V) ⇌ Water(l, lower V), ΔH > 0 ⇒ High P & High T favor melting
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Solubility of Gases in Liquids: Dissoln of gas in liquid is exothermic, so gas solubility increases with high pressure and decreases with rising temp. ▸ Gas(g) + Solvent(l) ⇌ Gas(aq), ΔH < 0 ⇒ Favored by High P and Low T
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Arrhenius, Brønsted-Lowry, and Lewis Acid-Base Theories: Arrhenius: H⁺/OH⁻ donor in water; Brønsted-Lowry: proton (H⁺) donor/acceptor. ▸ All Brønsted bases are Lewis bases, but not all Lewis acids are Brønsted acids
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs: Differ by a single proton (H⁺); a strong acid has a weak conjugate base, and a weak acid has a strong conjugate base. ▸ Acid ⇌ H⁺ + Conjugate Base; K_a × K_b(conjugate) = K_w = 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
Amphiprotic (Amphoteric) Anions: Species capable of both donating and accepting a proton depending on the reaction partner. ▸ H₂O, HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻, HPO₄²⁻, HS⁻ (Note: H₂PO₂⁻ is NOT amphiprotic!)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
Why H₂PO₂⁻ is NOT Amphiprotic: Hypophosphorous acid (H₃PO₂) is monobasic, so H₂PO₂⁻ can only accept H⁺. ▸ H₃PO₂ (monobasic) → H₂PO₂⁻ (only Brønsted base); H₃PO₃ (dibasic) → HPO₃²⁻
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
Classification of Lewis Acids: Electron-deficient molecules, cations,atoms with vacant d-orbitals, and polar π-systems. ▸ Lewis Acids: BF₃, BCl₃, AlCl₃, FeCl₃, SiF₄, SnCl₄, CO₂, SO₃, Ag⁺
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Ostwald's Dilution Law for Weak Electrolytes: For a weak monoprotic acid HA (K_a = Cα² / (1 − α) ≈ Cα²), degree of dissociation α increases upon dilution (V ↑ or C ↓). ▸ α = √(K_a / C) = √(K_a · V) (valid when α ≤ 0.05)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Ionic Product of Water (K_w): Product of molar conc.s of H⁺ and OH⁻ ions; at 298 K, K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ M², and increases with temp. ▸ K_w = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K; At 373 K, K_w ≈ 10⁻¹² (neutral pH = 6.0)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
Sørensen's pH and pOH Scale: Negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen or hydroxide ion activity; at 298 K, pH + pOH = pK_w = 14. ▸ pH = −log[H⁺]; pOH = −log[OH⁻]; pH + pOH = pK_w = 14 (at 298 K)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
pH of Very Dilute Strong Acid (e.g., 10⁻⁸ M HCl): Must include H⁺ from autoionization of water. ▸ 10⁻⁸ M HCl at 298 K ⇒ [H⁺] ≈ 10⁻⁷ + 10⁻⁸ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ M ⇒ pH ≈ 6.96
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
pH of a Weak Monoprotic Acid Solution: For weak acid HA of concentration C with α ≪ 1, hydrogen ion concentration is √(K_a · C). ▸ [H⁺] = Cα = √(K_a · C) ⇒ pH = ½ (pK_a − log C)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium
pH of a Mixture of Two Weak Acids: When two weak acids HA₁ (C₁, K_a1) and HA₂ (C₂, K_a2) are mixed in the same solution, common H⁺ ion suppresses both dissociations. ▸ [H⁺] = √(K_a1 C₁ + K_a2 C₂)
XI Ch 6: Equilibrium

Pauling's Rule for Successive pK_a of Oxoacids H_n XO_m: For an oxoacid written as XO_p(OH)_q, pK_a1 depends on the no. of non-protonated oxo groups p: p=0, p=1, p=2, p=3. ▸ XO_p(OH)_q: p=0 (HClO, H₃BO₃, Te(OH)₆)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Classical & Electronic Definitions of Redox: Oxidation is loss of e⁻ (or gain of O / loss of H); Reduction is gain of e⁻ (or loss of O / gain of H). ▸ OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of e⁻; Reduction Is Gain of e⁻
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidizing Agent vs Reducing Agent: An oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced; a reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized. ▸ Oxidant: Oxidation number decreases; Reductant: Oxidation number increases
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions
Oxidation Number of Elements in Free State: Atoms in elementary or allotropic forms have an oxidation state of exactly zero. ▸ OS = 0 in H₂, O₂, O₃, P₄, S₈, C(graphite/diamond), Na, Fe
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidation States of Fluorine and Other Halogens: Fluorine is the most EN element and ALWAYS exhibits −1 OS in all its compounds. ▸ OS(F) = −1 always; Exception: HOF is written with F = −1, H = +1, O = 0
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidation States of Oxygen in Oxides, Peroxides & Superoxides: Oxygen is −2 in normal oxides, −1 in peroxides, −½ in superoxides, +1 in O₂F₂, and +2 in OF₂. ▸ O²⁻ (−2), O₂²⁻ (−1), O₂⁻ (−0.5), O₂F₂ (+1), OF₂ (+2)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions
Oxidation States of Hydrogen: Hydrogen is +1 when bonded to non-metals and −1 in ionic metallic hydrides of Group 1 and Group 2. ▸ OS(H) = +1 in HCl, H₂O, NH₃; OS(H) = −1 in NaH, LiH, CaH₂
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Maximum & Minimum Oxidation Number Limits: For p-block elements, maximum OS equals group valence electrons (Group − 10) and minimum OS equals (Group − 18). ▸ N (Gp 15): −3 to +5; S (Gp 16): −2 to +6; Cl (Gp 17): −1 to +7
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Highest Known Oxidation State in Periodic Table: Osmium and Ruthenium exhibit +8 OS in their volatile tetroxides OsO₄ and RuO₄; Manganese reaches +7 in KMnO₄. ▸ OsO₄ & RuO₄: +8; KMnO₄ & Cl₂O₇: +7; K₂Cr₂O₇ & SF₆: +6
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions
Oxidation State of Cr in CrO₅ (Blue Perchromate): Calculated average is +10, but true OS is +6. ▸ CrO₅: x + 4(−1) + 1(−2) = 0 ⇒ OS(Cr) = +6 (Butterfly structure)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidation State of S in Caro's Acid & Marshall's Acid: Both peroxyacids contain one peroxy linkage, so sulfur remains in its maximum +6 OS. ▸ H₂SO₅: 2(+1) + x + 3(−2) + 2(−1) = 0 ⇒ OS(S) = +6; H₂S₂O₈: OS(S) = +6
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Paradox of Fractional Oxidation States: C₃O₂: In O=C=C=C=O, average OS of C is +4/3, whereas terminal carbons are +2 each and the central carbon is 0. ▸ C₃O₂: Terminal C = +2, Central C = 0 (Average = +4/3)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Fractional Oxidation State in Tribromooctaoxide: Average OS of Br is +16/3; the two terminal Br atoms bonded to three =O groups are +6 each. ▸ Br₃O₈: Two terminal Br = +6, Central Br = +4 (Average = +16/3)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidation States in Fe₃O₄, Pb₃O₄, and KI₃: Fe₃O₄ is a mixed oxide FeO·Fe₂O₃; Pb₃O₄ is 2PbO·PbO₂; in I₃⁻, two I atoms are 0 and one is −1. ▸ Fe₃O₄: one Fe²⁺ & two Fe³⁺ (avg +8/3); Pb₃O₄: two Pb²⁺ & one Pb⁴⁺ (avg +8/3)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidation States of N in NH₄NO₃ and NH₄NO₂: In ammonium nitrate (NH₄⁺NO₃⁻), nitrogen is −3 in NH₄⁺ and +5 in NO₃⁻ (avg = +1); in NH₄NO₂, N is −3 and +3 (avg = 0). ▸ NH₄NO₃: N = −3 and +5; NH₄NO₂: N = −3 and +3
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions
Oxidation State of Chlorine in Bleaching Powder: Bleaching powder is a mixed salt Ca(OCl)Cl containing hypochlorite ion and chloride ion. ▸ Ca(OCl)Cl: Cl in OCl⁻ = +1; Cl in Cl⁻ = −1 (Average = 0)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidation State of Carbon in HCN vs HNC: In both hydrogen cyanide (H−C≡N) and hydrogen isocyanide (H−N⁺≡C⁻), carbon has an oxidation state of +2 and nitrogen is −3. ▸ HCN & HNC: OS(H) = +1, OS(C) = +2, OS(N) = −3
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidation State of Metal in Metal Carbonyls: Carbon monoxide is a neutral ligand, so the transition metal in homoleptic metal carbonyls has zero oxidation state. ▸ OS = 0 in [Ni(CO)₄], [Fe(CO)₅], [Cr(CO)₆], [Mn₂(CO)₁₀]
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidation State of Fe in Brown Ring Complex: In [Fe(H₂O)₅(NO)]SO₄, nitric oxide acts as nitrosonium cation (NO⁺), so iron is in the unusual +1 OS. ▸ [Fe(H₂O)₅(NO⁺)]²⁺SO₄²⁻ ⇒ OS(Fe) = +1 (3 unpaired e⁻, μ = 3.87 BM)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Stock Notation for Transition Metal Compounds: Roman numerals in parentheses immediately after the metal name denote its OS. ▸ HAuCl₄ → Tetrachloridoauric(III) acid; Fe₂O₃ → Iron(III) oxide; SnCl₂ → Tin(II) chloride
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Compound Acting purely as Oxidant vs Reductant vs Both: Element in its highest OS acts only as oxidant; in lowest OS only as reductant ▸ Both Oxidant & Reductant: H₂O₂ (O = −1), SO₂ (S = +4), HNO₂ (N = +3), O₃
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Equivalent Weight of Oxidizing or Reducing Agent: Equals molar mass divided by n-factor (total number of electrons gained or lost per formula unit of substance). ▸ Equivalent Weight (E) = Molar Mass (M) / n-factor
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

n-Factor of KMnO₄ in Acidic, Neutral & Strongly Alkaline Media: MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺ in acid, MnO₂ in neutral/faintly alkaline. ▸ KMnO₄ E = M/5 (Acid: 158/5 = 31.6), M/3 (Neutral: 52.67), M/1 (Conc. OH⁻: 158)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

n-Factor of Potassium Dichromate in Acidic Medium: Each Cr₂O₇²⁻ (two Cr at +6) is reduced to 2Cr³⁺ (+3), gaining 2 × 3 = 6 e⁻ per mole of K₂Cr₂O₇. ▸ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O ⇒ n-factor = 6 (E = 294 / 6 = 49)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions
Combination Redox Reaction: Two reactants combine to form a single compound, where at least one reactant must be in its elemental form. ▸ C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g); 3Mg(s) + N₂(g) → Mg₃N₂(s)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Decomposition Redox Reaction: A compound breaks down into two or more components, at least one of which is in the elemental state. ▸ 2KClO₃(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O₂(g) (Note: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ is NOT redox!)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Non-Redox Thermal Decompositions: Decomposition of metal carbonates (CaCO₃) and ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl → NH₃ + HCl) involves zero change in oxidation states. ▸ CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) ⇒ Non-redox reaction
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Metal Displacement Redox Reaction: A more electropositive metal displaces a less active metal ion from its aq. salt soln or oxide (e.g., Thermite rxn). ▸ Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s); Cr₂O₃ + 2Al → Al₂O₃ + 2Cr
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions
Hydrogen Displacement from Cold Water, Steam, and Acids: Alkali/alkaline earth metals displace H₂ from cold water; Mg, Fe, Zn displace H₂ from steam/acids. ▸ 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Halogen Displacement Reaction Order: Oxidizing power of halogens decreases down Group 17, so an upper halogen displaces lower halide ions from aq. soln. ▸ Oxidizing Power: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ (Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions
Why Fluorine Cannot Be Prepared by Chemical Oxidation of F⁻: F₂ is the strongest chemical oxidizing agent. ▸ 2F⁻ → F₂ + 2e⁻ requires electrolysis of anhydrous KF + HF
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions
Disproportionation (Auto-Redox) Reaction: A single element in an intermediate oxidation state is simultaneously oxidized and reduced. ▸ 2H₂O₂ (O = −1) → 2H₂O (O = −2) + O₂ (O = 0)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Why Fluorine Never Undergoes Disproportionation: Being the most EN element, fluorine shows only 0 and −1 OSs and can never attain a positive OS. ▸ F₂ + OH⁻ cannot disproportionate (instead gives OF₂ or O₂ with F⁻)
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Reaction of Fluorine with Cold Dilute vs Hot Conc. NaOH: With cold dilute(2%) NaOH, F₂ forms oxygen difluoride (OF₂); with hot conc. NaOH, F₂ oxidizes water/hydroxide to O₂ gas. ▸ 2F₂ + 2NaOH(dil) → OF₂ + 2NaF + H₂O
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Disproportionation of Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ in Cold Dilute Alkali: Halogens (X = Cl, Br, I) disproportionate in cold dilute NaOH from 0 to −1 (halide) and +1 (hypohalite). ▸ Cl₂ + 2OH⁻(cold, dil) → Cl⁻ (−1) + ClO⁻ (+1) + H₂O
XI Ch 7: Redox Reactions

Oxidation State of Carbon in Glucose, Sucrose & Acetic Acid: Average OS of C is 0 in formaldehyde (HCHO), acetic acid, and glucose; −4 in CH₄. ▸ Average OS(C) = 0 in HCHO, CH₃COOH, C₆H₁₂O₆; −2 in C₂H₅OH
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Wöhler's Synthesis of Urea (1828): Disproved the Vital Force Theory by synthesizing organic urea from inorganic ammonium cyanate on heating. ▸ NH₄CNO (Ammonium cyanate) + Δ → NH₂CONH₂ (Urea)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Percentage s-Character & Electronegativity of Hybridized Carbon: As s-character increases from sp³ to sp, carbon becomes more EN. ▸ EN & Acidity: sp (50% s) > sp² (33.3% s) > sp³ (25% s)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Degree of Unsaturation: Number of rings plus pi bonds in a molecule of formula C_c H_h N_n O_o X_x. ▸ DBE = C + 1 − (H + X − N) / 2
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Classification of Heterocyclic Compounds: Furan, thiophene, pyrrole, and pyridine are aromatic heterocycles. ▸ Aromatic Heterocycles (6π e⁻): Furan (O), Thiophene (S), Pyrrole (NH), Pyridine (N)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Homologous Series Characteristics: Successive members differ by a −CH₂− unit, share the same general formula and functional group. ▸ Adjacent homologues differ by −CH₂− group and 14 u molar mass
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
IUPAC Priority Order of Principal Functional Groups: Highest priority group forms the principal suffix. ▸ −COOH > −SO₃H > −COOR > −COCl > −CONH₂ > −CN > −CHO > >C=O > −OH > −NH₂ > C=C > C≡C
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Groups Always Treated as Prefixes in IUPAC Nomenclature: Halogens, nitro, nitroso, alkoxy, and alkyl/aryl groups have no suffix. ▸ Always Prefixes: −F, −Cl, −Br, −I (halo), −NO₂ (nitro), −NO (nitroso), −OR (alkoxy)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
IUPAC Naming of C=C vs C≡C Tie-Breaker Rule: Double and triple bonds have equal priority for lowest locant set. ▸ HC≡C−CH₂−CH=CH₂ → Pent-1-en-4-yne (NOT Pent-4-en-1-yne)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Prefix vs Suffix Names of Common Functional Groups: When subordinate to a higher-priority group: −CN is cyano, −CHO is formyl, >C=O is oxo. ▸ −COOH: carboxy / -oic acid; −COCl: chlorocarbonyl / -oyl chloride
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
IUPAC Rule for Three or More Identical Terminal Functional Groups: When 3+ identical groups attach directly to an unbranched chain. ▸ Propane-1,2,3-tricarboxylic acid (Citric acid core)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
IUPAC Names of Important Benzene Derivatives: Anisole, Aniline, Toluene, Cumene, Styrene. ▸ Acetophenone: 1- Phenylethan-1-one; Benzophenone: Diphenylmethanone
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Number of 1°, 2°, 3°, and 4° Carbons in Isooctane: 2,2,4-Trimethylpentane contains five 1° carbons, one 2° carbon, one 3° carbon, and one 4° carbon. ▸ (CH₃)₃C−CH₂−CH(CH₃)₂ → 1°C = 5, 2°C = 1, 3°C = 1, 4°C = 1
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Alkyl Group Isomers: Propyl & Butyl Radicals: Propyl has 2 isomers (n-propyl, isopropyl); butyl (C₄H₉−) has 4 isomers. ▸ tert- Butyl = 1,1-Dimethylethyl; Isobutyl = 2-Methylpropyl; sec-Butyl = 1-Methylpropyl
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Vinyl, Allyl, Benzyl, Benzal & Benzo Groups: Vinyl is CH₂=CH−; Allyl is CH₂=CH−CH₂−; Benzyl is C₆H₅CH₂−; Benzal is C₆H₅CH<; Benzo is C₆H₅C≡. ▸ Vinyl chloride: Chloroethene; Allyl alcohol: Prop-2-en-1-ol
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Tropone and Tropolone Aromaticity: Non-benzenoid seven-membered ring compounds containing a 6π-electron tropylium-like delocalized system. ▸ Tropylium cation (C₇H₇⁺): Planar sp², 6π electrons, Hückel aromatic
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Chain, Position, and Functional Isomerism: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity: chain (C-skeleton), position (locant), or functional group. ▸ Propan-1-ol & Propan-2-ol (Position)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Important Functional Isomer Pairs for NEET: Alcohols & Ethers (C_n H_(2n+2)O); Aldehydes & Ketones (C_n H_(2n)O); Acids & Esters (C_n H_(2n)O₂). ▸ Nitroalkanes & Alkyl nitrites; Alkenes & Cycloalkanes
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Metamerism Condition & Examples: Arises due to unequal alkyl chains on either side of a polyvalent functional group. ▸ C₂H₅−O−C₂H₅ (Diethyl ether) and CH₃−O−C₃H₇ (Methyl propyl ether) are metamers
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Tautomerism (Keto-Enol Dynamic Equilibrium): Rapid interconversion involving migration of an α-hydrogen (sp³ C−H) across a conjugated X=Y−Z−H triad. ▸ CH₃−CO−CH₃ (Keto, >99.9%) ⇌ CH₂=C(OH)−CH₃ (Enol, <0.1%)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Enol Content Order in Carbonyl & β-Dicarbonyl Compounds: Enol content increases with conjugation, intramol. H-bonding, and aromaticity. ▸ Enol %: CH₃CHO < CH₃COCH₃ < CH₃COCH₂COOC₂H₅ < CH₃COCH₂COCH₃ < PhCOCH₂COPh < Phenol
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Geometrical Isomerism Conditions: Requires restricted rotation AND two different groups on each restricted atom (a ≠ b and d ≠ e). ▸ abC=Cde shows geometrical isomerism; a₂C=Cde does NOT
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Cahn-Ingold-Prelog (CIP) E-Z Nomenclature: Assign priority by atomic no. of directly attached atom; Z = high priorities together, E = opposite. ▸ Higher atomic number (or isotope mass: T > D > H) gets higher CIP priority
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Physical Properties of cis vs trans Isomers: cis-Isomer generally has higher dipole moment and higher boiling point. ▸ Boiling Point & μ: cis > trans
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Exception in Dipole Moment of 1-Chloropropene: In 1-chloropropene, the trans-isomer has a larger dipole moment. ▸ 1- Chloropropene & But-2-enoic acid: μ(trans) > μ(cis)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Number of Geometrical Isomers in Polyenes: For unsymmetrical polyene with n stereogenic double bonds, GI = 2^n. ▸ Unsymmetrical: GI = 2^n
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Specific Rotation [α] Formula (Biot's Law): Observed rotation α divided by path length l (in decimetres, 1 dm = 10 cm) and concentration c (in g mL⁻¹). ▸ [α]_D^T = α_obs / (l_dm × c_(g/mL))
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Diastereomers vs Enantiomers: Stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images of each other have different physical properties. ▸ Diastereomers can be separated by fractional distillation or chromatography
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Meso Compounds & Internal Compensation: Contain two or more chiral centers with an internal plane or center of symmetry (σ or i) ▸ meso-Tartaric acid (2R,3S): 2 chiral carbons, plane of symmetry, optically inactive
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Racemic Mixture & External Compensation: Equimolar (50:50) mixture of d and l enantiomers; optically inactive due to external compensation. ▸ Racemic (±) mixture: Net rotation = 0° (External compensation)
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Calculation of Optical Isomers: For unsymmetrical molecule with n chiral centers: d/l isomers = 2^n, meso = 0. ▸ Tartaric acid (symmetrical, n=2): 2 active (d, l) + 1 meso = 3 stereoisomers
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Chiral Molecules Without a Chiral Carbon: Even-cumulenes and ortho-tetrasubstituted biphenyls with bulky groups show optical activity. ▸ 2,3-Pentadiene and 6,6'-Dinitrodiphenic acid are chiral without asymmetric carbon
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Number of Structural Isomers of Alkanes: Methane, ethane, propane have 1; butane (C₄H₁₀) = 2; pentane (C₅H₁₂) = 3; hexane (C₆H₁₄) = 5; heptane (C₇H₁₆) = 9. ▸ Alkane structural isomers: C₄=2, C₅=3, C₆=5, C₇=9, C₈=18
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
Number of Structural Isomers of C₄H₁₀O and C₅H₁₁Cl: C₄H₁₀O has 7 structural isomers; C₄H₈ has 5 chain/position/ring isomers. ▸ C₄H₁₀O: 4 alcohols + 3 ethers = 7
XI Ch 8: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

Lassaigne's Test for Nitrogen in Diazonium Salts & Hydrazine: Hydrazine has no carbon so NaCN cannot form unless charcoal/ starch. ▸ NH₂NH₂ + Na + Charcoal (C) → NaCN (gives positive Prussian blue test only if C is added)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Sabatier-Senderens Hydrogenation of Alkenes & Alkynes: Catalytic addition of H₂ over finely divided Pt/Pd/Ni at room temp. ▸ R−CH=CH₂ + H₂ --(Pt/Pd/Ni)--> R−CH₂−CH₃ (Syn addition of H₂)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Wurtz Reaction for Symmetrical Alkanes: Alkyl halides react with metallic sodium in dry ether to yield symmetrical alkanes. ▸ 2R−X + 2Na --(Dry Ether)--> R−R + 2NaX (3° alkyl halides undergo elimination to alkenes)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Corey-House Alkane Synthesis: Coupling of lithium dialkylcuprate with a 1° alkyl halide (R'−X) synthesizes both symmetrical and unsymmetrical alkanes. ▸ R₂CuLi + R'−X → R−R' + R−Cu + LiX (works for odd and even C alkanes)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Soda-Lime Decarboxylation of Sodium Carboxylates: Heating sodium salt of a RCOOH with soda-lime yields an alkane with one fewer carbon atom. ▸ R−COONa + NaOH --(CaO, Δ)--> R−H + Na₂CO₃ (Rate ∝ stability of carbanion R⁻)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Kolbe's Electrolytic Method for Alkanes: Electrolysis of conc. aq. sodium/potassium carboxylate soln liberates symmetrical alkane. ▸ 2R−COONa + 2H₂O --(Electrolysis)--> R−R (anode) + 2CO₂ (anode) + H₂ (cathode) + 2NaOH
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Reduction of Alkyl Halides to Alkanes: Alkyl halides are reduced to alkanes by Zn + dil. HCl, LiAlH₄, or red P + HI at 423 K. ▸ R−X + Zn + H⁺ → R−H + Zn²⁺ + X⁻; R−I + HI --(Red P, 423 K)--> R−H + I₂
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Boiling Point Trend of Isomeric Alkanes: Boiling point increases with mol. mass and decreases with branching. ▸ Boiling Point of C₅H₁₂: n-Pentane (309.1 K) > Isopentane (300.9 K) > Neopentane (282.5 K)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Melting Point Alternation & Symmetry in Alkanes: Alkanes with an even no. of carbon atoms pack more tightly in the crystal lattice. ▸ Melting Point of C₅H₁₂: Neopentane > n-Pentane (143.3 K) > Isopentane (113 K)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Reactivity Order of C−H Bonds in Free Radical Halogenation: Determined by ease of C−H homolysis: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₄. ▸ Relative Chlorination Rate at 298 K (1° : 2° : 3°) = 1 : 3.8 : 5.0
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Controlled Catalytic Oxidation of Alkanes: Methane + O₂ gives CH₃OH over Cu at 523 K/100 atm, HCHO over Mo₂O₃ + Δ. ▸ 2CH₄ + O₂ --(Cu, 523K/100atm)--> 2CH₃OH; CH₄ + O₂ --(Mo₂O₃, Δ)--> HCHO + H₂O
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Oxidation of Tertiary Alkanes with KMnO₄: Alkanes normally resist KMnO₄ oxidation. ▸ (CH₃)₃C−H (Isobutane) + [O] --(KMnO₄)--> (CH₃)₃C−OH (2-Methylpropan-2-ol)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Isomerization of n-Alkanes: Heating n-alkanes with anhydrous AlCl₃ and HCl gas converts straight-chain alkanes into branched- chain isomers. ▸ n-Hexane --(Anhyd. AlCl₃ / HCl, Δ)--> 2-Methylpentane + 3-Methylpentane
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Aromatization of n-Alkanes: Heating n-alkanes having 6 or more carbons to 773 K at 10–20 atm over Cr₂O₃, V₂O₅. ▸ n-Hexane -- (Cr₂O₃/V₂O₅/Mo₂O₃, 773 K, 10–20 atm)--> Benzene + 4H₂ (n-Heptane → Toluene)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Steam Reforming of Methane (Syngas Production): Methane reacts with steam at 1273 K over a nickel catalyst to produce carbon monoxide and dihydrogen (synthesis gas). ▸ CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) --(Ni, 1273 K)--> CO(g) + 3H₂(g)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Pyrolysis (Thermal Cracking) of Alkanes: Free-radical thermal decomposition of higher alkanes into lower alkanes, alkenes, and H₂ at 773–973 K. ▸ C₆H₁₄ --(773 K)--> C₆H₁₂ + H₂ + C₄H₈ + C₂H₆ + C₃H₆ + C₂H₄ + CH₄
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Conformations of Ethane: Staggered conformation has minimum torsional strain and is more stable than eclipsed conformation by 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹. ▸ Stability in Ethane: Staggered (θ = 60°) > Skew > Eclipsed (θ = 0°)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Conformations of n-Butane (C₂–C₃ Rotation): Anti is most stable, then Gauche, Partially Eclipsed, and Fully Eclipsed. ▸ n-Butane Stability: Anti (180°) > Gauche (60°) > Partially Eclipsed (120°) > Fully Eclipsed
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Exception Where Gauche Conformer is More Stable Than Anti: In ethylene glycol, 2-fluoroethanol, and chlorohydrin. ▸ HO−CH₂−CH₂−OH & F−CH₂−CH₂−OH: Gauche > Anti (stabilized by intramol. H-bond)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Conformations of Cyclohexane & Baeyer Strain Theory: Chair conformation is free of angle and torsional strain; Twist-boat has lower energy than Boat. ▸ Cyclohexane Stability: Chair > Twist-Boat > Boat > Half-Chair
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Lindlar's Catalyst vs Birch Reduction of Internal Alkynes: Partial hydrogenation of R−C≡C−R' with H₂ / Pd-CaCO₃ gives cis- alkene; Na / liquid NH₃ gives trans-alkene. ▸ RC≡CR' --(H₂/Pd-CaCO₃)--> cis-Alkene
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Dehydrohalogenation of Alkyl Halides: Heating R−X with alcoholic KOH eliminates HX to form an alkene; rate follows 3° > 2° > 1° and R−I > R−Br > R−Cl. ▸ R−CH₂−CH₂−X + KOH(alc.) --(Δ)--> R−CH=CH₂ + KX + H₂O
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Saytzeff's Rule vs Hofmann Elimination: Normal dehydrohalogenation gives the more substituted, stable Saytzeff alkene as major product. ▸ 2-Bromobutane + alc. KOH → But-2-ene (80%, Saytzeff) + But-1-ene (20%, Hofmann)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Dehalogenation of Vicinal Dihalides with Zinc: Heating a vicinal dihalide with Zn dust in methanol/ethanol (or NaI in acetone) yields an alkene. ▸ R−CHBr−CH₂Br + Zn ----> R−CH=CH₂ + ZnBr₂
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Acid-Catalyzed Dehydration of Alcohols: Heating alcohols with conc. H₂SO₄ (or H₃PO₄ / Al₂O₃) forms an alkene via a carbocation intermediate. ▸ CH₃CH₂OH ----> CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Electrophilic Addition of Bromine: Reddish-brown Br₂ in CCl₄ adds across an alkene via a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate to yield a colorless vicinal. ▸ R−CH=CH₂ + Br₂(red-brown) --(CCl₄)--> R−CHBr−CH₂Br (colorless)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Markovnikov's Rule for HX Addition to Unsymmetrical Alkenes: In ionic addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene. ▸ CH₃−CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃−CH(Br)−CH₃ (2-Bromopropane, major via 2° carbocation)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Kharasch Peroxide Effect: With organic peroxide (PhCO−O−O−COPh), ONLY HBr adds to unsymmetrical alkenes via a free- radical mechanism to give the 1° anti-Markovnikov bromide. ▸ CH₃−CH=CH₂ + HBr ----> CH₃−CH₂−CH₂−Br
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Why HCl and HI Do NOT Show the Peroxide Effect: For HCl, cleavage of the strong H−Cl bond (430 kJ/mol) by alkyl radical is endothermic. ▸ Only HBr has both propagation steps exothermic
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Hydration of Alkenes: Acid-Catalyzed, Oxymercuration & Hydroboration: Acid-catalyzed hydration (H₃O⁺) gives Markovnikov alcohol with carbocation rearrangement. ▸ H₃O⁺: Markovnikov (rearranges)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Baeyer's Reagent Hydroxylation: Cold dilute neutral/alkaline KMnO₄ decolorizes with an alkene via stereospecific SYN dihydroxylation to give a vicinal cis-diol. ▸ CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + [O] ----> HO−CH₂−CH₂−OH + MnO₂↓ (brown)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Oxidative Cleavage of Alkenes with Hot Acidic KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇: Hot acidified KMnO₄ cleaves C=C completely: =CH₂ is oxidized to CO₂ + H₂O. ▸ (CH₃)₂C=CH−CH₃ --(KMnO₄ / H⁺, Δ)--> (CH₃)₂C=O (Acetone) + CH₃COOH (Acetic acid)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Reductive Ozonolysis of Alkenes: Alkene reacts with O₃ to form an ozonide, which on reductive cleavage with Zn + H₂O replaces C=C with two C=O groups without further oxidation. ▸ R−CH=CR'₂ ----> R−CHO + R'₂C=O + ZnO
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Allylic Bromination / Chlorination: N-Bromosuccinimide (NBS) in CCl₄ with hν/peroxide, or Cl₂ at high temp. ▸ CH₃−CH=CH₂ + NBS (or Cl₂ at 773 K) → Br−CH₂−CH=CH₂ (Allyl bromide / 3-Bromopropene)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons

Ziegler-Natta Polymerization Catalyst: Combination of triethylaluminium [(C₂H₅)₃Al] and titanium tetrachloride (TiCl₄) catalyzes. ▸ Ziegler-Natta Catalyst: (C₂H₅)₃Al + TiCl₄ (Low T & P → linear high-density polythene)
XI Ch 9: Hydrocarbons
Directive Influence of Nitroso and Styryl Groups: Although −N=O and −CH=CH−COOH are net e⁻-withdrawing (−I). ▸ −F, −Cl, −Br, −I, −N=O, −CH=CH₂, −CH=CH−COOH are deactivating yet ortho/para-directing
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Amalgam & Solid-Gas Solution Examples: Mercury in sodium (solid) is a liquid-in-solid soln; H₂ gas in palladium is a gas-in-solid soln. ▸ Hg in Na: Liquid in Solid; Chloroform in N₂: Liquid in Gas
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Composition of Brass, Bronze & German Silver: Brass is Cu (70%) + Zn (30%); Bronze is Cu (90%) + Sn (10%); German silver is Cu + Zn + Ni. ▸ German Silver = Cu + Zn + Ni (0% Ag); Bronze = Cu + Sn; Brass = Cu + Zn
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Toxicity of Fluoride Ion Concentration in Water: 1.0 ppm of F⁻ in drinking water prevents tooth decay, 1.5 ppm causes mottled teeth, and high conc.s are used as rat poison. ▸ 1.0 ppm F⁻: Prevents tooth decay
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Effect of Temperature on Dissolution of Solid in Liquid: By Le Chatelier's principle, solubility increases with temp. ▸ Δ_sol H > 0 (KNO₃, NaCl): T ↑ ⇒ Solubility ↑
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Effect of Temperature on Solubility of Gases in Liquids: Dissoln of a gas in a liquid is an exothermic process. ▸ Aquatic species prefer cold water over warm water due to higher dissolved O₂ content
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Henry's Law for Gas Solubility in a Liquid: At constant temp., the partial pressure (p) of a gas in the vapour phase is ∝ its mole fraction (x). ▸ p = K_H · x (where K_H is Henry's law constant, with units of bar or atm)
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Characteristics of Henry's Law Constant (K_H): K_H depends on the nature of gas and solvent and INCREASES with temp. ▸ T ↑ ⇒ K_H ↑ ⇒ Gas Solubility (x = p / K_H) ↓
XII Ch 1: Solutions

K_H Values of He, H₂, N₂, O₂, and CO₂ in Water: At 298 K, He and N₂ have much higher K_H than O₂ and CO₂, so He and N₂ are far less soluble. ▸ Solubility in water: CO₂ > O₂ > H₂ > N₂ > He (inverse order of K_H)
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Scuba Diving (Decompression Sickness / 'The Bends'): Under high underwater pressure, N₂ dissolves in blood and forms painful bubbles upon surfacing. ▸ Scuba tank mixture: 11.7% He + 56.2% N₂ + 32.1% O₂
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Anoxia at High Altitude & Carbonated Beverages: Low partial pressure of O₂ at high altitudes lowers blood O₂ conc. ▸ Anoxia = Low blood [O₂] at high altitude due to low atmospheric p_(O₂)
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Vapour Pressure of a Pure Liquid: Eqm pressure exerted by vapour above a liquid at a given temp.; depends ONLY on nature of liquid and temp. ▸ Stronger intermol. forces ⇒ Lower vapour pressure & Higher Δ_vap H
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Raoult's Law for Two Volatile Liquids: Partial vapour pressure of each volatile component in a soln equals its pure vapour pressure multiplied by its mole fraction in the liquid phase. ▸ p₁ = p₁° x₁ and p₂ = p₂° x₂
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Raoult's Law as a Special Case of Henry's Law: Both laws state p_i ∝ x_i; they differ only in the proportionality constant. ▸ Raoult's Law: p_i = p_i° x_i; Henry's Law: p_i = K_H x_i
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Raoult's Law for Non-Volatile Solute in Volatile Solvent: Adding a non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent. ▸ P_soln = p₁ = p₁° x₁ ⇒ (p₁° − p₁) / p₁° = 1 − x₁ = x₂ (Relative Lowering of V.P.)
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Ideal Solution Thermodynamic Criteria: Obeys Raoult's law at all conc.s and temp.s; A–B intermol. attractions equal A–A and B– B attractions. ▸ Ideal Soln: ΔH_mix = 0, ΔV_mix = 0, ΔS_mix > 0, ΔG_mix < 0
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Classic Examples of Ideal Liquid Solutions: Chemically similar homologues or structural analogues form nearly ideal solns. ▸ n- Hexane + n-Heptane; Benzene + Toluene; Bromoethane + Chloroethane
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Positive Deviation from Raoult's Law Criteria: Occurs when A–B intermol. attractions are WEAKER than A–A and B–B attractions. ▸ Positive Deviation: p_i > p_i° x_i, ΔH_mix > 0, ΔV_mix > 0, ΔS_mix > 0, ΔG_mix < 0
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Examples of Solutions Showing Positive Deviation: Mixtures where adding a non-polar liquid breaks strong H-bonds or dipole interactions. ▸ Ethanol + Water; Ethanol + Acetone; Ethanol + Cyclohexane; CS₂ + Acetone
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Examples of Solutions Showing Negative Deviation: Mixtures that form new intermol. H-bonds or undergo acid-base association on mixing. ▸ Chloroform + Acetone; Phenol + Aniline; Water + Strong Acid (HNO₃, HCl, H₂SO₄)
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Why Chloroform + Acetone Shows Negative Deviation: The slightly acidic C−H hydrogen of CHCl₃ forms a new intermol. ▸ Cl₃C−H···O=C(CH₃)₂ H-bond ⇒ ΔH_mix < 0, ΔV_mix < 0, P_total < P_Raoult
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Azeotropes (Constant-Boiling Mixtures): Binary mixtures having the same composition in liquid and vapour phases that boil at a constant temp. ▸ At azeotropic composition: x₁ = y₁ and x₂ = y₂
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Minimum-Boiling Azeotropes: Formed by solns showing large POSITIVE deviation from Raoult's law at a specific composition. ▸ 95.5% Ethanol + 4.5% Water (B.P. 351.15 K < 351.5 K of pure EtOH)
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Plot of 1 / P_total vs Vapour-Phase Mole Fraction: While P_total vs liquid mole fraction (x₁) is linear for an ideal soln. ▸ 1 / P_total = (1 / p₂°) + [(p₁° − p₂°) / (p₁° p₂°)] y₁
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Ostwald-Walker Dynamic Method for Vapour Pressure: Dry air is passed successively through soln, pure solvent (loss w₂ ∝ P° − P_s), and CaCl₂ drying tube (gain w₁ + w₂ ∝ P°). ▸ (P° − P_s) / P° = w₂ / (w₁ + w₂) = x_solute
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Lowering of Vapour Pressure vs Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure: Lowering of V.P. depends on both temp. and x₂; Relative Lowering is a colligative property independent of temp. ▸ Δp = p₁° x₂ (depends on T)
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Exact Relation Between Relative Lowering of V.P. and Molality: Since x₂ = n₂ /, rearranging / p₁ gives an exact linear relationship with molality. ▸ (p₁° − p₁) / p₁ = n₂ / n₁ = (w₂ M₁) / (M₂ w₁) = m × (M₁ / 1000)
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Steam Distillation Vapour Pressure Formula: For two completely immiscible liquids, each exerts its pure vapour pressure independently so the mixture boils below 373 K. ▸ P_total = p°_water + p°_organic = P_atm
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Solubility Curve Inflection of Glauber's Salt: Solubility increases up to 32.4 °C and then decreases above 32.4 °C as endothermic decahydrate. ▸ At 32.4 °C: Na₂SO₄·10H₂O (Δ_sol H > 0) → Na₂SO₄(s) (Δ_sol H < 0) + 10H₂O
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Raoult's Law at Equal Moles of Two Volatile Liquids: For an equimolar ideal mixture of two volatile liquids A and B. ▸ When n_A = n_B (x_A = x_B = 0.5): P_total = ½ (p_A° + p_B°)
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Entropy and Gibbs Energy Change in All Liquid Solutions: Whether a soln is ideal or shows positive or negative deviation. ▸ For ALL true solns (Ideal, +ve dev., −ve dev.): ΔS_mix > 0 and ΔG_mix < 0
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Colligative Properties Definition: Properties of dilute solns that depend solely on the number (conc.) of solute particles. ▸ 4 Colligative Properties: RLVP (Δp/p₁°), ΔT_b, ΔT_f, and Osmotic Pressure (Π)
XII Ch 1: Solutions

Ebullioscopic Constant: Elevation in boiling point for a 1 molal (1 mol kg⁻¹) ideal non-electrolyte soln; depends ONLY on the nature of the SOLVENT. ▸ Units of K_b (and K_f) = K kg mol⁻¹; For water: K_b = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Thermodynamic Formula for Ebullioscopic Constant: Derived from Clausius-Clapeyron relation using solvent molar mass M₁. ▸ K_b = (R · M₁ · (T_b°)²) / (1000 × Δ_vap H) = (R · (T_b°)²) / (1000 × l_vap)
XII Ch 1: Solutions
Why Water Boils at 373.15 K at 1 atm vs 372.78 K at 1 bar: Because 1 bar is slightly lower than 1 atm. ▸ Boiling point of pure water: 100 °C (373.15 K) at 1 atm (1.013 bar)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Electrochemical Cell: Galvanic cell converts chemical energy of a spontaneous redox rxn (ΔG < 0) into electrical energy. ▸ Galvanic: Anode is (−)ve, Cathode is (+)ve
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
LOAN Mnemonic for Galvanic Cell: Left side, Oxidation, Anode, Negative terminal; e⁻ flow externally from Anode to Cathode. ▸ LOAN: Left = Oxidation = Anode = Negative (in Galvanic cell)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Effect of Opposing External Potential on Daniell Cell: When E_ext < 1.1 V, cell acts as galvanic cell; when E_ext = 1.1 V, no current flows. ▸ E_ext < 1.1 V: Galvanic
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

IUPAC Cell Notation & Cell Potential Formula: Anode half-cell is written on the left and cathode on the right separated by a salt. ▸ E°_cell = E°_right(cathode) − E°_left(anode) (using standard reduction potentials)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Relation Between Cell EMF, Gibbs Energy, and Equilibrium Constant: Maximum electrical work equals −Δ_r G = nFE_cell; under standard conditions at 298 K, Δ_r G° = −nFE°_cell = −2.303 RT log K_c. ▸ Δ_r G° = −n F E°_cell
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Nernst Equation for Half-Cell Reduction Potential: For M^(n+)(aq) + ne⁻ → M(s), electrode reduction potential increases with metal ion conc. ▸ E_(M^(n+)/M) = E°_(M^(n+)/M) − log(1 / [M^(n+)]) = E° + log[M^(n+)]
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Cell Potential at Chemical Equilibrium: When a galvanic cell reaches chemical eqm (discharged battery), Q = K_c and the net cell potential drops to zero. ▸ At eqm: E_cell = 0 and Δ_r G = 0 ⇒ E°_cell = (0.0591 / n) log K_c
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Nernst Potential of Hydrogen Electrode vs pH at 298 K: For 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g, 1 bar) with E° = 0 V, reduction potential is directly proportional to minus pH. ▸ E_(H⁺/H₂) = −0.0591 × pH (at P_(H₂) = 1 bar and 298 K)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Concentration Cell EMF Formula: In an electrolyte conc. cell M | M^(n+)(C₁) || M^(n+)(C₂) | M, E°_cell = 0. ▸ E_cell = (0.0591 / n) log(C₂ / C₁) (Spontaneous when C_cathode > C_anode)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Temperature Coefficient of Cell EMF_P: By Gibbs-Helmholtz equation, entropy change of the cell rxn equals nF times the temp. coefficient of cell EMF. ▸ ΔS = n F (∂E_cell / ∂T)_P; ΔH = −n F [E_cell − T (∂E_cell / ∂T)_P]
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Calomel Reference Electrode & Silver-Silver Chloride Electrode: Secondary reference electrodes with accurately known stable potentials. ▸ Calomel Electrode: Hg(l) | Hg₂Cl₂(s) | Cl⁻(aq) (Secondary reference electrode)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Resistance, Conductance, and Cell Constant: Resistance R = ρ(l/A); Conductance G = 1/R; Cell constant G* = l/A. ▸ G = 1 / R = κ × (A / l) = κ / G* ⇒ Conductivity κ = G × G*
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Specific Conductance / Conductivity (κ, Kappa): Conductance of a unit cube of electrolyte soln. ▸ κ = (1 / R) × (l / A); Units of κ = S cm⁻¹ or S m⁻¹ (1 S cm⁻¹ = 100 S m⁻¹)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Metallic vs Electrolytic Conduction: Metallic conduction occurs via e⁻ without chemical change and DECREASES with rising temp. ▸ T ↑ ⇒ Metallic conductivity ↓
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Molar Conductivity Definition & Practical Formula: Conducting power of all ions produced by 1 mole of electrolyte in soln of molarity M (mol L⁻¹). ▸ Λ_m = (κ × 1000) / M (in S cm² mol⁻¹ when κ is in S cm⁻¹)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Effect of Dilution on Conductivity vs Molar Conductivity: On dilution: specific conductivity κ ALWAYS DECREASES. ▸ On Dilution: κ DECREASES, whereas Λ_m and Λ_eq INCREASE
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Debye-Hückel-Onsager Equation for Strong Electrolytes: For strong electrolytes, Λ_m increases slowly and linearly as √C. ▸ Λ_m = Λ_m° − A √C (Plot of Λ_m vs √C is a straight line with slope −A and y-intercept Λ_m°)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Variation of Λ_m with √C for Weak Electrolytes: For weak electrolytes, Λ_m rises steeply at high dilution as degree. ▸ Weak electrolyte: Steep non-linear rise at low √C ⇒ Λ_m° must be calculated using Kohlrausch
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Kohlrausch's Law of Independent Migration of Ions: At infinite dilution (C → 0), each ion migrates independently of its co-ion and makes a definite contribution. ▸ For A_x B_y: Λ_m° = x λ°_(A^(y+)) + y λ°_(B^(x−))
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Calculating Λ_m° of Acetic Acid Using Kohlrausch's Law: Obtained algebraically from the limiting molar conductivities of strong electrolytes CH₃COONa, HCl. ▸ Λ_m°(CH₃COOH) = Λ_m°(CH₃COONa) + Λ_m°(HCl) − Λ_m°(NaCl)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Calculating Λ_m° of NH₄OH and BaSO₄ Using Kohlrausch's Law: For NH₄OH, combine NH₄Cl + NaOH − NaCl; for BaSO₄, combine BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ − 2NaCl. ▸ Λ_m°(NH₄OH) = Λ_m°(NH₄Cl) + Λ_m°(NaOH) − Λ_m°(NaCl)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Exceptionally High Ionic Conductivity of H⁺ and OH⁻ in Water: In aq. soln, H⁺ and OH⁻ have the highest conductivities due to proton hopping along H-bonds. ▸ Aq. Ionic Mobility Order: H⁺ ≫ OH⁻ > Cs⁺ > Rb⁺ > K⁺ > Na⁺ > Li⁺
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Degree of Dissociation and K_a from Conductance: For a weak electrolyte at molarity C, α equals Λ_m / Λ_m°. ▸ α = Λ_m / Λ_m°; K_a = (C α²) / (1 − α) = (C Λ_m²) / [Λ_m° (Λ_m° − Λ_m)]
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Solubility and K_sp of Sparingly Soluble Salt from Conductance: A saturated soln of a sparingly soluble salt is so dilute that Λ_m ≈ Λ_m°. ▸ S = (κ_salt × 1000) / Λ_m° (in mol L⁻¹)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Wheatstone Bridge Measurement of Electrolytic Resistance: Uses an alternating current (AC) oscillator and a headphone/null detector with platinized Pt electrodes. ▸ AC source prevents polarization and electrolysis
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Conductometric Titration: Strong Acid vs Strong Base: Conductance initially falls sharply up to the equivalence point. ▸ HCl vs NaOH Conductometric curve: V-shaped minimum at equivalence point
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Conductometric Titration: Weak Acid vs Strong Base: Conductance starts very low, rises slowly as un-ionized CH₃COOH converts to ionic. ▸ CH₃COOH vs NaOH: Slow linear rise before equivalence point, steep rise after
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Ionic Mobility and Transport Number: Ionic mobility is drift velocity per unit electric field (u = v / E = λ° / F) ▸ u = λ° / (z · F); t_+ = λ°_+ / (λ°_+ + λ°_-); t_+ + t_- = 1
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Conductivity Water Ionic Product from κ: Using κ_water = 5.5 × 10⁻⁸ S cm⁻¹ and Λ_m°(H₂O) = λ°(H⁺) + λ°(OH⁻) = 349.6 + 199.1 = 548.7 S cm² mol⁻¹ gives [H⁺]. ▸ [H⁺] = (κ_water × 1000) / (λ°_H⁺ + λ°_OH⁻) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis: Mass (w) of substance deposited or liberated at any electrode is ∝ the quantity of electric charge passed. ▸ w = Z · Q = Z · I · t = (E / 96500) · I · t = (M / (n × 96500)) · I · t
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Electrochemical Equivalent & 1 Faraday of Charge: 1 Faraday is the charge on 1 mole of e⁻ and always deposits 1 gram- equivalent of any substance. ▸ 1 F = 96500 C mol⁻¹ deposits 1 g-eq = (1/n) mole of substance
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry
Faraday's Second Law of Electrolysis: When the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes connected in series. ▸ w₁ / w₂ = E₁ / E₂ = Z₁ / Z₂ ⇔ (n₁ × moles₁) = (n₂ × moles₂)
XII Ch 2: Electrochemistry

Effect of Adding NH₃ or CN⁻ to Cu²⁺ Half-Cell on Its Reduction Potential: Adding NH₃ or KCN to the Cu²⁺ | Cu half-cell ties up free Cu²⁺ ions. ▸ Complexation of M^(n+) lowers free [M^(n+)] and decreases E_red(M^(n+)/M)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Average and Instantaneous Rate of a Chemical Reaction: For aA + bB → cC + dD, rate of rxn equals rate of disappearance or appearance of any. ▸ Rate = −(1/a)(d[A]/dt) = −(1/b)(d[B]/dt) = +(1/c)(d[C]/dt) = +(1/d)(d[D]/dt)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Units of Rate of a Chemical Reaction: Concentration per unit time: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ (or M s⁻¹) in solution, and atm s⁻¹ or bar s⁻¹ for gas- phase reactions. ▸ Rate in pressure units = (dP/dt) = RT × (dC/dt)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
Rate Law & Specific Reaction Rate: Experimentally determined equation relating rxn rate to molar conc.s of reactants raised to powers x and y. ▸ Rate = k [A]^x [B]^y
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Characteristics of Rate Constant: k depends on the nature of rxn, temp. (increases with T), and catalyst; k is INDEPENDENT of reactant conc.s! ▸ k depends on T and Catalyst (E_a); k is independent of [Reactants]
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Units of k for Zero, First, Second, and Third Order Reactions: Zero order (n=0): mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; First order (n=1): s⁻¹; Second order (n=2): L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. ▸ n=0: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; n=1: s⁻¹; n=2: L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; n=3: L² mol⁻² s⁻¹
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Order of a Reaction Characteristics: Sum of exponents of reactant conc.s in the experimentally determined rate law. ▸ Order is an experimental quantity (applicable to both elementary and complex rxns)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Molecularity of an Elementary Reaction: No. of reacting species that must collide simultaneously in a SINGLE elementary step to bring about a chemical rxn. ▸ Molecularity is a theoretical whole number (1, 2, or rarely 3)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Why Molecularity Greater Than 3 Is Rarely Observed: The probability of more than three molecules colliding simultaneously. ▸ Molecularity > 3 is not observed due to negligible probability of simultaneous 4-body collision
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Rate-Determining Step in Complex Multi-Step Reactions: The overall rate of a complex multi-step rxn is controlled by its SLOWEST elementary step. ▸ Overall Rate of complex rxn = Rate of slowest step (RDS)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Reaction Mechanism with Fast Pre-Equilibrium Before Slow RDS: When the slow RDS involves a reactive intermediate formed in a fast reversible pre-eqm, substitute the intermediate conc. ▸ For 2O₃ → 3O₂: Fast: O₃ ⇌ O₂ + O
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
Fractional Order Reaction Examples: Thermal decomposition of acetaldehyde CH₃CHO → CH₄ + CO has order 1.5 (Rate = k[CH₃CHO]^(3/2)). ▸ CH₃CHO pyrolysis: Order = 1.5
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Photochemical Reaction of H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: Photochemical combination of H₂ and Cl₂ over water surface in sunlight is a ZERO- order rxn whose rate depends on light intensity (I_a). ▸ H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) --(hν, over H₂O)--> 2HCl
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
First-Order Reaction Classic Examples: All natural & artificial radioactive decays, decomposition of N₂O₅, N₂O, H₂O₂, SO₂Cl₂. ▸ 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ and 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ follow First-Order kinetics
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
Pseudo-First-Order Reaction Definition & Examples: A bimolecular rxn that behaves as first-order. ▸ Pseudo-1st-Order: Acid- catalyzed hydrolysis of Ethyl acetate & Inversion of Cane sugar
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Inversion of Cane Sugar (Sucrose Hydrolysis): Dextrorotatory sucrose hydrolyzes in acid to an equimolar mixture of D-(+)- glucose and D-(−)-fructose. ▸ C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O --(H⁺)--> C₆H₁₂O₆(Glc) + C₆H₁₂O₆(Fru)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
Initial Rate Method: Comparing initial rates r₁ and r₂ at two initial conc.s [A]₁ and [A]₂ determines the partial order x. ▸ r₂ / r₁ = ([A]₂ / [A]₁)^x ⇒ x = log(r₂ / r₁) / log([A]₂ / [A]₁)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

General Half-Life Dependence on Initial Concentration [A]₀: For an n-th order rxn, the half-life t_1/2 is ∝ 1/ [A]₀ raised. ▸ t_1/2 ∝ 1 / ([A]₀)^(n−1) (Ostwald's isolation / half-life method for finding order n)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
Zero-Order Integrated Rate Equation: Differential rate −d[A]/dt = k integrates to a linear decrease in reactant conc. with time. ▸ [A]_t = [A]₀ − k t ⇒ k = ([A]₀ − [A]_t) / t
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
Zero-Order Half-Life (t_1/2) & Lifetime (t_100%): Half-life of a zero-order rxn is ∝ initial reactant conc. ▸ Zero-order: t_1/2 = [A]₀ / (2k); t_100% = [A]₀ / k = 2 × t_1/2
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

First-Order Time Milestones: Because each half-life reduces the remaining reactant by ½, key fractional completion times follow exact multiples. ▸ t_75% = 2 × t_1/2; t_87.5% = 3 × t_1/2; t_90% = 3.32 × t_1/2 (or 2.303/k)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
First-Order Rate Equation Between Two Arbitrary Times t₁ and t₂: If conc.s are [A]₁ at time t₁ and [A]₂ at time t₂. ▸ k = [2.303 / (t₂ − t₁)] log([A]₁ / [A]₂)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Average Life of a First-Order / Radioactive Decay: Reciprocal of the first-order decay constant k; equals the time in which the conc. drops to 1/e (36.8%) of its initial value. ▸ τ = 1 / k = t_1/2 / 0.693 = 1.44 × t_1/2
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
Linear Plots for First-Order Reactions: Plot of ln[A]_t vs t has slope = −k and intercept = ln[A]₀; Plot of log[A]_t vs t has slope = −k / 2.303. ▸ Slope of log[A]_t vs t = −k / 2.303
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

First-Order Gas-Phase Reaction in Terms of Total Pressure: A → B + C: For A(g) → B(g) + C(g) with initial pressure P_i and total pressure P_t = P_i + x. ▸ For A(g) → B(g) + C(g): k = (2.303 / t) log[ P_i / (2P_i − P_t) ]
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
First-Order Decomposition of H₂O₂ Monitored by KMnO₄ Titration: When equal aliquots of decomposing H₂O₂ are titrated against standard KMnO₄. ▸ k = (2.303 / t) log(V₀ / V_t)
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

First-Order Acid Hydrolysis of Ester Monitored by NaOH Titration: Alkali NaOH neutralizes both the constant acid catalyst and the acetic acid produced. ▸ k = (2.303 / t) log[ (V_∞ − V₀) / (V_∞ − V_t) ]
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

First-Order Inversion of Sucrose Monitored by Polarimeter: If r₀ is initial rotation, r_t is rotation at time t, and r_∞ is final rotation at completion. ▸ k = (2.303 / t) log[ (r₀ − r_∞) / (r_t − r_∞) ]
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Second-Order Integrated Rate Equation & Half-Life: For 2A → Products with Rate = k[A]², the reciprocal of conc. (1/[A]_t) increases linearly with time t, and half-life is ∝ 1/ [A]₀. ▸ 1/[A]_t − 1/[A]₀ = k t
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
Parallel First-Order Reactions: A → B and A → C: Effective decay constant is k_eff = k₁ + k₂; effective half-life is 0.693 / (k₁ + k₂) ▸ k_eff = k₁ + k₂; % of B = [k₁ / (k₁ + k₂)] × 100
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics
Temperature Coefficient of a Reaction (μ): Ratio of rate constants at two temp.s differing by 10 K (usually k_(308 K) / k_(298 K)). ▸ Temp. Coefficient μ = k_(T + 10) / k_T ≈ 2 to 3
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Why Reaction Rate Doubles for Every 10 K Rise in Temperature: A 10 K rise increases mean kinetic energy by only 3%. ▸ Area under Maxwell-Boltzmann curve beyond E_a (e^(−E_a/RT)) doubles for a 10 K rise
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Maxwell-Boltzmann Energy Distribution Curve & Most Probable Kinetic Energy: Peak of the distribution curve gives the most probable kinetic energy. ▸ As T ↑: Peak (most probable KE) shifts right and downward
XII Ch 3: Chemical Kinetics

Logarithmic Form of Arrhenius Equation & Linear Plot: Taking log₁₀ of the Arrhenius equation shows that a plot of log k vs 1/T is a straight line with a negative slope. ▸ log k = log A − [E_a / (2.303 R)] · (1 / T)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Transition Element IUPAC Definition & Group 12 Exception: A transition element has an incompletely filled d-subshell in its ground state. ▸ Zn (3d¹⁰4s²), Cd (4d¹⁰5s²), Hg (5d¹⁰6s²) → Non-transition d-block elements
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Four Transition Series & Element Ranges: 3d series: Sc(21) to Zn(30) [Period 4]; 4d series: Y(39) to Cd(48) [Period 5]. ▸ 3d: Sc– Zn; 4d: Y–Cd; 5d: La(57), Hf(72)–Hg(80); 6d: Ac(89), Rf(104)–Cn(112)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Anomalous Electronic Configurations in 3d Series: Extra stability of half-filled (3d⁵) and completely filled (3d¹⁰) subshells. ▸ Cr (Z=24): [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Anomalous Configurations in 4d and 5d Series: Palladium is unique in having ZERO outer s-e⁻; Mo(42) is 4d⁵5s¹, Ag(47) is 4d¹⁰5s¹, Pt(78) is 4f¹⁴5d⁹6s¹, and Au(79) is 4f¹⁴5d¹⁰6s¹. ▸ Pd (Z=46): [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Melting Point & Enthalpy of Atomization Trend in d-Block: Peaks near the middle of each series. ▸ Zn (692.7 K), Cd (594 K), and Hg have lowest M.P. and Δ_a H°

Dip in Melting Point of Manganese & Technetium: Despite having 5 unpaired e⁻, Mn shows an anomalously sharp dip in melting point. ▸ 3d M.P. peak at Cr (2180 K), sharp dip at Mn (1519 K), second peak at Fe (1811 K)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Enthalpy of Atomization Order: 5d > 4d > 3d Series: Heavy transition metals of the 4d and 5d series have significantly higher enthalpies of atomization than 3d elements. ▸ Δ_a H°: 5d series > 4d series > 3d series
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Atomic and Ionic Radii Trend Across 3d Series: Decreases from Sc to Cr, remains nearly constant from Fe, Co, Ni, and increases slightly at Cu and Zn. ▸ 3d Atomic Radius: Sc > Ti > V > Cr > Mn > Fe ≈ Co ≈ Ni < Cu < Zn
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Lanthanoid Contraction Effect on 4d vs 5d Atomic Radii: Filling of poor-shielding 4f orbitals before 5d causes 5d elements to have nearly IDENTICAL atomic and ionic radii to the corresponding. ▸ Zr (160 pm) ≈ Hf (159 pm)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Density Trend Across the 3d Series & Highest Density Elements: Across the 3d series, atomic volume decreases while atomic mass increases. ▸ 3d Density: Sc < Ti < V < Cr < Mn < Fe < Co < Ni < Cu > Zn
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Ionization Enthalpy Anomalies in 3d Series: Zn has the highest IE₁ in 3d (3d¹⁰4s²); Cr and Cu have the highest IE₂ in their vicinity; Mn and Zn have very high IE₃. ▸ IE₂: Cu > Ni and Cr > Mn
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Variable Oxidation States of 3d Elements: Arise because both (n−1)d and ns orbitals have very similar energies; minimum OS equals no. of 4s e⁻, and maximum OS up to Mn equals. ▸ Mn shows widest range in 3d: +2 to +7
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Elements Showing ONLY ONE Non-Zero Oxidation State in 3d Series: Scandium exhibits only +3, and Zinc exhibits only +2 (3d¹⁰). ▸ Only +3 in 3d: Sc (Sc³⁺); Only +2 in 3d: Zn (Zn²⁺)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Stability of Higher Oxidation States: 4d/5d vs 3d Elements: In p-block, lower OS is more stable for heavier elements (inert pair effect) ▸ Mo(VI) and W(VI) are stable, whereas Cr(VI) (K₂Cr₂O₇) is a strong oxidizing agent!
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Highest Oxidation States Stabilized by Fluorine and Oxygen: Fluorine stabilizes high OS due to high lattice/bond energy (VF₅, CrF₆, MnF₄) ▸ Highest fluoride of Mn is MnF₄ (+4), whereas highest oxide is Mn₂O₇ (+7)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Why Cr²⁺ Is a Strong Reducing Agent While Mn³⁺ Is a Strong Oxidizing Agent: Both Cr²⁺ and Mn³⁺ have d⁴ config.: Cr²⁺ readily oxidizes to Cr³⁺. ▸ Cr²⁺ (d⁴ → d³, t_2g³): Strong reducing agent (liberates H₂ from dil. acid)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Stability of Cu²⁺(aq) Over Cu⁺(aq) in Water: In gaseous state Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) is more stable. ▸ Δ_hyd H°(Cu²⁺) is much more exothermic than Δ_hyd H°(Cu⁺) ⇒ Cu²⁺(aq) is more stable than Cu⁺
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Instability of CuI₂, Cu₂, and FeI₃: Cu²⁺ oxidizes I⁻ to I₂ and CN⁻ to cyanogen (CN)₂, precipitating white Cu₂I₂ and CuCN; similarly, Fe³⁺ oxidizes I⁻ to I₂, so FeI₃ does not exist. ▸ 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂↓ (white) + I₂
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Copper Halides Stability vs Copper Halides: All Cu(II) halides exist except CuI₂; for Cu(I), CuF is unstable, while insoluble Cu₂Cl₂, Cu₂Br₂, and Cu₂I₂ are stable covalent solids. ▸ CuI₂ does not exist; CuF is unstable
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Diamagnetic vs Maximum Paramagnetic 3d Ions: Ions with d⁰ and d¹⁰ (Cu⁺, Zn²⁺) have n = 0 (μ = 0, diamagnetic); Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) and Mn²⁺ (3d⁵) have maximum n = 5 (μ = 5.92 BM). ▸ Diamagnetic (n=0): Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺, Zn²⁺
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Origin of Colour in Transition Metal Ions: Ions with partially filled d-orbitals absorb visible light to promote an e⁻ from lower-energy to higher-energy split. ▸ Colourless (d⁰ or d¹⁰): Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cu⁺, Zn²⁺, Cd²⁺
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Charge-Transfer Spectra: Although Mn(VII) in KMnO₄ and Cr(VI) in K₂Cr₂O₇/K₂CrO₄ have 3d⁰ config., they are intensely coloured. ▸ LMCT: MnO₄⁻, Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange), CrO₄²⁻ (yellow), MnO₄²⁻
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Catalytic Properties of Transition Metals & Compounds: Due to ability to adopt variable OSs and provide large surface area with vacant d-orbitals. ▸ V₂O₅, Fe (Haber), Ni, TiCl₄ + Al(C₂H₅)₃, PdCl₂ (Wacker), Fe²⁺ + H₂O₂
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Reaction of Iodide with Persulphate Catalyzed by Fe³⁺: In 2I⁻ + S₂O₈²⁻ → I₂ + 2SO₄²⁻, Fe³⁺ catalyzes the rxn by alternating between +3. ▸ Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ redox cycle lowers E_a for rxn between two negatively charged anions
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Alloy Formation Criterion: Transition metals readily form homogeneous solid-soln alloys with one another when their atomic radii. ▸ Alloys formed when atomic radii differ by ≤ 15% (e.g., Stainless steel = Fe + Cr + Ni)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Nature of Transition Metal Oxides with Oxidation State: For a transition metal, ionic and basic character of oxides decreases while covalent and acidic character increases as OS increases. ▸ MnO → Mn₂O₃/Mn₃O₄/MnO₂ → Mn₂O₇
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Oxides of Chromium & Vanadium Acid-Base Trend: CrO (+2) is basic; Cr₂O₃ (+3) is amphoteric. ▸ CrO (basic), Cr₂O₃ (amphoteric), CrO₃ (acidic)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Preparation of Potassium Dichromate from Chromite Ore: Three steps: (1) Fusion of chromite ore with Na₂CO₃ + air gives yellow Na₂CrO₄ (and Fe₂O₃) ▸ 4FeCr₂O₄ + 8Na₂CO₃ + 7O₂ → 8Na₂CrO₄ (yellow) + 2Fe₂O₃ + 8CO₂
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Why K₂Cr₂O₇ rather than Na₂Cr₂O₇ Is Used as Primary Standard in Volumetric Analysis: Sodium dichromate is deliquescent and cannot be weighed accurately. ▸ Na₂Cr₂O₇ is deliquescent (hygroscopic)
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Oxidizing Action of Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ Half-Reaction: In acidic soln, orange dichromate ion is reduced to green Cr³⁺ ion. ▸ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ (green) + 7H₂O
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements

Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ + H₂O₂: Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ reacts with H₂O₂ to form deep blue chromium(VI) peroxide, which is extracted and stabilized in ether. ▸ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2H⁺ + 4H₂O₂ --(Ether)--> 2CrO₅ (Deep blue, Cr = +6) + 5H₂O
XII Ch 4: The d- and f-Block Elements
Why KMnO₄ Solution Is Stored in Dark Brown Bottles: Aq. KMnO₄ decomposes slowly with sunlight into MnO₂, KOH. ▸ Dark bottles prevent sunlight-catalyzed decomposition of MnO₄⁻ to MnO₂
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds
Werner's Coordination Theory: Primary vs Secondary Valency: Primary valency is the ionizable OS. ▸ Primary valency = OS (ionizable); Secondary valency = Coord. number (directional)
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds
Denticity of Ligands: Unidentate, Didentate & Polydentate: No. of donor atoms in a single ligand that simultaneously coord. to the central metal atom. ▸ Unidentate (1): H₂O, NH₃, CO, Cl⁻, CN⁻
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds
Symmetric vs Unsymmetric Didentate Ligands: Ethane-1,2-diamine (en: H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂) and oxalate (C₂O₄²⁻) have two identical donor atoms (symmetric, AA) ▸ en (N,N) and ox²⁻ (O,O) are symmetric (AA)
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds
EDTA⁴⁻ Hexadentate Ligand: EDTA⁴⁻ is a hexadentate ligand possessing 6 donor sites: 2 nitrogen donor atoms and 4 carboxylate (−COO⁻) oxygen donor atoms. ▸ EDTA⁴⁻: Hexadentate (2 N + 4 O donors)
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds
Chelate Effect & Thermodynamic Origin: Didentate or polydentate ligands form cyclic ring structures around the metal ion. ▸ [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 3 en → [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ + 6 H₂O
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds

Ambidentate Ligands Definition & Classic Examples: Unidentate ligands possessing two different nucleophilic donor atoms, either of which can coord. to the metal ion. ▸ Ambidentate: NO₂⁻, SCN⁻, CN⁻, S₂O₃²⁻
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds

Flexidentate Ligands: Polydentate ligands that do not always use all their donor atoms and can exhibit variable denticity depending on the complex. ▸ SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻, NO₃⁻ can act as unidentate or didentate
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds
Homoleptic vs Heteroleptic Complexes: Homoleptic complexes contain only one type of donor group/ligand (e.g., [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺, [Ni(CO)₄], [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻) ▸ Homoleptic: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds
IUPAC Nomenclature Rules for Coordination Compounds: Cation is named first, then anion; inside the coord. ▸ Neutral/ Cationic complex: Metal uses standard name (Cobalt, Iron, Platinum)
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds

Special IUPAC Ligand Names: H₂O = aqua, NH₃ = ammine, CO = carbonyl, NO = nitrosyl, Cl⁻ = chlorido, CN⁻ = cyanido, OH⁻ = hydroxido. ▸ Complex ligands with numbers in name use bis-, tris-, tetrakis- with parentheses
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds

IUPAC Names of Key NCERT Complexes: [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl(NO₂)] is Diamminechloridonitrito-N-platinum(II); K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃] is Potassium trioxalatochromate(III) ▸ [Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃] = Iron(III) hexacyanidoferrate(II)
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds
Effective Atomic Number Rule: Total e⁻ around the central metal ion in a complex tend to equal the atomic no. of the next noble gas: EAN = Z − + 2 ×. ▸ EAN = Z − OS + 2(CN)
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds

Ionization Isomerism: Same overall formula, but exchange of an anionic ligand inside the coord. sphere with a counter-ion outside gives different ions in aq. soln. ▸ [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Br and [Co(NH₃)₅Br]SO₄
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds

Solvate / Hydrate Isomerism: Special type of ionization isomerism where water molecules act either as coordinating aqua ligands inside the sphere or as water. ▸ [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ vs [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O vs [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O
XII Ch 5: Coordination Compounds
Linkage Isomerism: Arises when an ambidentate ligand (NO₂⁻, SCN⁻, CN⁻) coord.s to the central metal through different donor atoms. ▸ [Co(NH₃)₅(NO₂)]Cl₂ vs [Co(NH₃)₅(ONO)]Cl₂

Sandmeyer Reaction & Gattermann Reaction for Haloarenes: Treating cold benzenediazonium chloride with Cu₂Cl₂/HCl or Cu₂Br₂/HBr or Cu powder + HCl/HBr yields. ▸ C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ --(Cu₂X₂ / HX)--> C₆H₅−X + N₂↑ (X = Cl, Br)

C−X Bond Length, Bond Enthalpy & Dipole Moment of Methyl Halides: As halogen size increases from F to I, C−X bond length increases and bond dissociation enthalpy decreases. ▸ Bond Length: C−F < C−Cl < C−Br < C−I
XII Ch 6: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
